0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
Second Peter is the apostle's last will and testament. Writing in the shadow of his own death — 'the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me' (1:14; cf. John 21:18–19) — Peter addresses a church under pressure from false teachers who have crept inside the community, twisted Paul's letters, and weaponized a crude uniformitarianism against the hope of Christ's return. The letter's three movements answer three threats: the erosion of moral seriousness (ch. 1: grow in the divine nature), the corruption of doctrine by immoral teachers (ch. 2: their condemnation is certain), and the mocking of eschatological hope (ch. 3: the Day is coming and it will be unlike anything the world has seen).

The letter's authorship is the most contested in the NT canon. The vocabulary differs sharply from 1 Peter, and Origen already noted that some doubted it. Eusebius placed it among the antilegomena — letters known but disputed. Yet the arguments for Petrine authorship are substantial: the self-identification is unusually specific (Simeon Peter, v.1; the eyewitness claim of vv.16–18; the reference to a prior letter in 3:1); a forger who fabricates this much personal detail is extraordinarily bold. The vocabulary difference most likely reflects a different secretary — 1 Peter was written dia Silouanou (through Silvanus, 1 Pet 5:12), while 2 Peter's quite different style may reflect Peter writing without that help, or with another. The church ultimately recognized it as canonical, and its theological weight — the virtue chain, the transfiguration testimony, the patience of God, the new creation — fully justifies that recognition.

The relationship to Jude is unavoidable: 2 Peter 2 and Jude share extensive material (the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, the Balaam archetype, waterless clouds, the scoffers of the last days). The majority of scholars believe Peter used Jude (not the reverse), which, if correct, places 2 Peter after Jude and in the mid-to-late 60s AD — consistent with Peter's death under Nero (c. 64–68 AD). Peter does not merely copy Jude; he develops, expands, and re-focuses the material for a church whose crisis has moved from external pressure to internal corruption.

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence,<sup>4</sup>by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.<sup>5</sup>For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge,<sup>6</sup>and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness,<sup>7</sup>and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.<sup>8</sup>For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>9</sup>For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.<sup>10</sup>Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall.<sup>11</sup>For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.<sup>12</sup>Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have.<sup>13</sup>I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder,<sup>14</sup>since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.<sup>15</sup>And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.<sup>16</sup>For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.<sup>17</sup>For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,"<sup>18</sup>we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.<sup>19</sup>And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,<sup>20</sup>knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation.<sup>21</sup>For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
1.overview:
Chapter 1 lays the foundation. God’s power has already given believers everything they need for life and godliness (v. 3). On that gift rests the command: make every effort to add to your faith, and so confirm your calling (vv. 5, 10). Gift first, then effort: that is the grammar of grace.

The second half grounds Peter’s message in two witnesses that agree: the apostles saw Christ’s glory at the transfiguration, and the prophetic Scriptures, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit, point to the same Christ and his coming day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to believers whose faith is of equal value to his own. God’s power has given them everything for life and godliness, and his promises make them sharers in his holy nature. So they must make every effort to grow in a chain of qualities from faith to love. Those who grow are kept from fruitlessness and confirm that God has called them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Partakers of the Divine Nature

God’s power has already granted everything needed for life and godliness. Sharing the divine nature means sharing his holiness, not becoming God, and growth in the qualities of verses 5–7 is how a believer confirms his calling.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter told readers who had seen nothing that their faith was of equal standing with his.

Now: When growth stalls, look first for a memory of forgiveness that has grown dim (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Peter 1 lays the foundation for resisting false teachers: true knowledge of Christ, growing character, and the sure word of Scripture. Peter greets those who share an equal faith through the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ (vv. 1–2). God’s power has given us everything for life and godliness through knowing him, and by his promises we share the divine nature (vv. 3–4). So believers add to faith a chain of virtues ending in love (vv. 5–7); those who lack them are blind and have forgotten their cleansing (vv. 8–9). Be diligent to confirm your calling and election, and you will receive a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom (vv. 10–11). Facing death, Peter keeps reminding them (vv. 12–15). The message is no myth: they saw Christ’s majesty on the holy mountain and heard the Father’s voice (vv. 16–18). And Scripture is a lamp in a dark place, for men spoke from God, carried along by the Holy Spirit (vv. 19–21).

The setting. Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome around AD 64–68, shortly before, as early tradition holds, his martyrdom under Nero. (Many scholars date it later and doubt that Peter wrote it; the textual note below sets out why, and why this commentary receives it as his.) It addresses the same churches as 1 Peter (3:1). Its main concern is false teachers within the churches who denied Christ’s return and lived immorally (chapters 2–3). Chapter 2 closely parallels the letter of Jude. The first letter was written to Christians suffering from outside; this one to Christians endangered from inside. Persecution can kill the body, but false teaching can empty a church while leaving its building full, and Peter, with the executioner not far off, judged it the greater danger.

Simeon Peter. The first word is unexpected. Not Simon, the ordinary Greek form, but Symeōn, the old Hebrew form, the name of a patriarch. (Some manuscripts read Simon, and the KJV follows them.) It appears this way of Peter only once elsewhere in the New Testament, on the lips of James at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:14). Then both names together: the one he was born with and the one Jesus gave him, Petros, rock. A man writing his last letter signs it with his whole history: the fisherman who sank in the lake and swore he did not know the man; and the rock, which he never became by his own strength but was made by the One who named him.

A servant and apostle. Servant first, doulos, a slave, and apostle second. The man who once argued about who was the greatest now introduces himself as the property of another. And the two words do not compete. Because he is Christ’s slave, he can speak with Christ’s authority: an apostle is a man sent with a message that is not his, and the only way to carry such a message faithfully is to have no ambitions of your own for it.

A faith of equal standing. The phrase is the letter’s opening kindness. Obtained, lachousin, is a word for receiving by lot: what falls to you rather than what you achieve, as the lot fell on Zechariah to burn incense (Luke 1:9). Faith is an allotment, a gift, not a prize won (Ephesians 2:8). Of equal standing, isotimon, means of the same value, the same honour. Peter had seen the Transfiguration and will describe it in fifteen verses; he tells readers who have seen nothing, probably mostly Gentiles who never heard Jesus’ voice, that their faith is of exactly equal worth to his. There is no first-class and second-class Christianity.

My faith feels nothing like an apostle’s. How can it be equal? Because faith is not valued by its strength but by its object. A weak hand and a strong hand receive the same gift; a trembling faith in a mighty Christ saves as surely as a bold one. What is equal is not your feelings, your knowledge or your record, but the Christ you hold and the righteousness given to you. Thomas, who doubted, and the thief, who believed in his last hours, received the same Saviour as Peter. So do not measure your standing by comparing your faith with other people’s. Measure it by whom you are trusting, and grow from there.

Our God and Savior Jesus Christ. In Greek a single article governs both nouns, a construction that normally marks them as one person. Peter calls Jesus God directly, as Paul does in Titus 2:13. Compare 1:11; 2:20; 3:18, where the same construction (“our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ”) plainly refers to one person: nobody has ever suggested that the Lord and the Saviour in those verses are two different people. It is one of the New Testament’s clearest statements of Christ’s deity, and it stands at the front door of a letter written against men who denied the Master who bought them (2:1). Righteousness, dikaiosynē, carries two shades together: God’s fairness in giving the same faith to all, Jew and Gentile, apostle and newcomer; and the righteousness of Christ himself, by which believers are justified. Justification is God the Judge pronouncing a person righteous: not making him sinless overnight, but counting him righteous because Christ’s perfect righteousness is credited to the one who trusts him (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). The faith is equal because the righteousness is his, and it is not divided into larger and smaller portions.

Grace and peace be multiplied. Not merely given but multiplied, as in 1 Peter 1:2, because the God who gives grace does not run short of it. Grace is God’s free favour; peace is what it produces: reconciliation with God and rest within.

In the knowledge of God. Here comes the letter’s key word. Knowledge, epignōsis, is full, personal, experiential knowledge, the knowing that belongs to a relationship rather than a library. It appears four times in this short letter (1:2, 3, 8; 2:20), and it is Peter’s answer to the false teachers, who were probably offering knowledge of another kind: secret, superior, liberating from ordinary morality. Peter does not answer them by despising knowledge. He names the true knowledge, the knowledge of God in Christ, and says it is here, in knowing him, that grace and peace grow.

Is this knowledge just a matter of learning doctrine? No, though it is never less than that. You cannot know a person while being wrong about who he is, so true doctrine matters. But Peter means knowing God the way a child knows his father: trusting him, hearing him, walking with him, and growing in that acquaintance over years. It comes through his word, through prayer, through the worship and fellowship of his people, and through obeying him and finding him faithful. A man can know a great deal about God and not know him; a simple believer may know little theology and know him truly. The aim is both: a mind that is accurate and a heart that is personally acquainted.

Textual note. 2 Peter was one of the most disputed books in the early church: early church writers report that some doubted it, and noticed that its style differs from 1 Peter. Most modern scholars think a follower wrote it in Peter’s name after his death, pointing to that difference of style, to its heavy use of the material in Jude, to its mention of Paul’s letters as a collection counted with the Scriptures (3:15–16), and to the complaint that the fathers have fallen asleep (3:4). These are real questions, and honest scholars weigh them differently. On the other side, the letter plainly claims to be from Peter, refers to the Transfiguration as an eyewitness (vv. 16–18), mentions Jesus’ prediction of Peter’s death (v. 14), and refers to a previous letter (3:1); the early church rejected writings it knew to be falsely attributed, and, after careful consideration, received this one. Differences of style may be due to a different secretary or none (Silvanus helped with 1 Peter, 1 Peter 5:12) and to a different subject. The question cannot be settled by proof either way. This commentary receives the letter as Peter’s, as the church long has, and as Scripture.

What it does not mean. “Equal standing” does not mean all believers have the same apostolic authority. It means the same saving faith, equally precious to God. Peter still writes as an apostle, and the readers still need to listen to him (3:2). Equality of faith is not equality of office.

On a Tuesday. If you know someone who feels like a second-class believer, the new convert with a chaotic past, the believer who cannot pray aloud, tell them what Peter told his readers: your faith is as precious as his.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome in the mid 60s AD. “Simeon” is the Hebrew form of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His divine power has granted. Granted, dedōrēmenēs, is perfect tense: has given, and it remains ours. Not supplied in instalments as needed, but already given in full. Divine power is the power of God at work through Christ, the power that raised him from the dead; life and godliness are spiritual life and the godly living that flows from it. And this sentence closes a door before the false teachers can open it. If everything necessary has been provided, then no supplementary knowledge is on offer, and anyone promising a further instalment is selling something that does not exist.

If I have everything, why do I feel I am lacking so much? Because having and using are different things. A man may inherit a great house and live in one room of it, cold and hungry, because he has never opened the other doors. Peter does not say you already feel complete or behave perfectly; he says the resources are yours. What you lack is not a new gift but growth in using the one you have: knowing Christ better, trusting his promises more, and practising what he has already made possible. That is why the next verses call for effort. So when someone offers you a secret, a second blessing, a technique or a special experience that will finally make the Christian life work, you may answer kindly: I have been given all things in Christ, and I need to know him better, not something besides him.

Him who called us. The channel is knowing a person, not acquiring information. Called, kalesantos, is God’s effectual call: not an invitation merely issued and left to us, but the summons that creates what it commands, as Jesus’ voice brought Lazarus out of the tomb.

His own glory and excellence. Glory, doxa, is the weight and radiance of who he is. Excellence, aretē, is moral goodness; the word was used of a god’s mighty deeds, and Peter used it in his first letter of the excellencies of the one who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9). The Greek can mean that God called us by his glory and excellence, drawn by his beauty as Peter himself was drawn when he fell at Jesus’ knees in the boat, or that he called us to share them. Probably both. He calls us into the very thing he is.

Precious and very great promises. Precious, timia, is his own recurring word: he used it of the trial of faith, of the blood of Christ, and of Christ the living stone (1 Peter 1:7, 19; 2:4–7). Very great, megista, is literally greatest. What promises? Forgiveness, the gift of the Spirit, eternal life, Christ’s return, the new heavens and new earth in which righteousness dwells (3:4, 9, 13). And they are given, not dangled. God has bound himself by his word, and every one of his promises finds its Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Partakers of the divine nature. Partakers, koinōnoi, is the word for business partners in Luke 5:10, where James and John were Simon’s partners in the fishing. Through God’s promises believers share in God’s own moral character and life: his holiness, love and goodness. This is the new birth (1 Peter 1:23; John 3:5–6), union with Christ (John 15:4–5), being renewed in his image (Colossians 3:10; Romans 8:29). It has been misread in both directions. It does not mean human beings become God, or are absorbed into deity: Scripture never blurs the line between the Creator and his creatures. Nor is it a poetic exaggeration meaning nothing much. God’s own life is truly in his people. The Holy Spirit lives in every believer (Romans 8:9), and he gives you desires that are God’s own, so that you begin to love what God loves, holiness, truth and his people, and to hate what he hates. You remain a creature, but you are no longer only what you were.

He shared ours. The way into this sharing runs through the incarnation. Since the children share in flesh and blood, Hebrews says, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14). The Son took our nature, without ceasing to be God, so that in union with him we might receive his life, without ceasing to be creatures. He entered a world of corruption without being corrupted, and by his death and rising broke its hold. Christians share the divine nature only because the divine Son first, and freely, shared the human one.

How can a promise make me share God’s nature? Because God’s promises are not information about a distant future; they are the means by which the Spirit unites us to Christ now. When you believe God’s promise that your sins are forgiven, you are freed from guilt and drawn to love him. When you believe that Christ is coming and you will be like him (1 John 3:2–3), you begin to purify yourself as he is pure. A promise believed changes what you want. That is how the new nature grows: not by striving to become divine, but by trusting what God has said, until his character is reproduced in yours.

Having escaped from the corruption. Escaped, apophygontes, means fled from, like a man running out of a burning building. Corruption, phthora, is decay, moral rot, the process by which something good goes bad; and the world’s rot comes from disordered desire (James 1:14–15). The clause defines the divine nature by its opposite: it is a promise of holiness and incorruption, not of divinity. Peter will use the same word of the false teachers, who promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption (2:19). There are only two directions: toward God’s life, or toward the rot.

In the flow. Verses 3–4 explain how grace and peace can be multiplied in the knowledge of God (v. 2). They are also the foundation for the rest of the chapter. Because God has given all (vv. 3–4), believers make every effort (vv. 5–11); because the gift must not be forgotten, Peter keeps reminding them (vv. 12–15); and because the promises rest on what God has said and done, he shows that the message is no myth (vv. 16–21). And the precious promises include the promise of Christ’s coming, the very one the scoffers of chapter 3 will mock (3:4, 13).

Where Christians differ: do believers become divine? Eastern Orthodoxy teaches theosis or deification, in which believers progressively become gods by grace; Orthodox theologians themselves insist that believers share God’s energies, his life and activity, never his essence, so the difference from Reformed teaching is real but narrower than it sounds. Some modern movements go further and teach that believers become little gods. Verdict: Believers share in God’s moral nature (his holiness, love and life) through union with Christ by the Spirit, but they never share in his essence, his deity, or his incommunicable attributes like omnipotence or omniscience. The Creator-creature distinction is never erased. We become like God in character, not God in being (1 John 3:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18).

On a Tuesday. Take one promise of God and carry it through the day. If you are anxious, his promise never to leave you (Hebrews 13:5); if you are tempted, his promise of a way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13); if you are guilty, his promise to forgive the one who confesses (1 John 1:9). When the desire that rots presses on you, answer it with what God has said.

For worship. God has not given us a starter kit and left us to complete the set. He has given everything, by his own divine power, and the gift remains. We were rotting in the world’s decay, and he brought us out. We were made of dust, and he will not make us gods, but he has made us his children, partakers of the life that has no end.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this very reason, make every effort. Because God has given you everything (vv. 3–4). The effort rests on a gift already complete, which is the New Testament’s constant order. Make every effort, spoudēn pasan pareisenenkantes, is literally bringing in all diligence alongside: God has brought everything; you bring your diligence beside it. Work out your salvation, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). Grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning. A man who has been given a farm does not earn it by ploughing, but he will certainly plough.

Supplement your faith with virtue. The verb, epichorēgēsate, is the chorēgos word: in Athens the chorēgos was the wealthy citizen who funded a chorus for the great festivals and paid for everything it needed, lavishly, at his own expense. Peter used the word of God’s supply in his first letter (1 Peter 4:11); here he asks the same generosity from them. Then eight qualities in a chain, each growing out of the last. It starts where it must: faith, which is not one link among others but the ground. The first quality built on it is virtue, aretē, moral excellence, the same word used of God in verse 3. God called us by his excellence, and now his excellence is to appear in us.

Knowledge. Gnōsis here is understanding and practical wisdom: knowing God’s will and how to apply it. It follows virtue because goodness without understanding blunders. Zeal without knowledge has done enormous damage in the church (Romans 10:2).

Self-control. Enkrateia is self-mastery, literally holding oneself in. It follows knowledge, since knowing what is right settles nothing until the appetites are governed. The false teachers had knowledge, or claimed it, without self-control (2:10–14), and Peter describes where that ends.

Steadfastness. Hypomonē is endurance, remaining under weight (James 1:3–4). It is self-control extended over time, which is a different and harder thing. Anyone can resist a temptation once. Steadfastness is resisting it on the four hundredth day, when the novelty of the fight has gone and the pressure has not.

Godliness. Eusebeia is reverence for God shown in life. It turns the whole sequence God-ward and prevents it becoming mere self-mastery. A Stoic philosopher could have admired the qualities so far. Godliness is what makes them Christian: everything done before God’s face, for his sake.

Brotherly affection. Philadelphia is family love for fellow believers: warmth, loyalty, enjoyment of one another, as children of the same Father. Godliness that does not love God’s children is not godliness (1 John 4:20).

Love. Agapē is self-giving love that reaches past the family to everyone, including enemies, the crown of the list (1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 3:14). The chain runs from what God has given, through the ordering of one’s own character, and out to other people, and it ends at love, the goal it has been moving toward. The last link is the one that looks most like Christ, who loved his own and also prayed for those who crucified him.

Is this effort not a kind of legalism? No. Legalism is effort to earn God’s favour or to add to Christ’s work. Peter’s effort springs from favour already given: because God has granted you everything, make every effort. The difference is the difference between a slave labouring to buy his freedom and a son working in his father’s fields. Both may sweat. Only one does it from rest. If you notice that your effort has become anxious, proud or joyless, the remedy is not to stop trying but to go back to verses 3–4 and remember what you have been given. There is a quieter danger too. A list of virtues can become a self-improvement project, pursued so that you can admire yourself or be admired. Peter’s chain guards against that at both ends: it begins with faith, which only receives, and ends with love, which gives itself away.

Must I master these qualities one at a time, in order? No. Peter is not describing a staircase where you finish one step before you begin the next. The links grow together, each strengthening the others, like branches on one tree. The order shows how they depend on one another: knowledge guides goodness, self-control keeps knowledge honest, endurance makes self-control last. But a young believer shows something of all of them from the start, and the oldest saint is still growing in every one.

What does adding self-control actually look like? Start with one appetite that rules you more than it should: food, the phone, anger, spending, sleep, lust. Decide in advance, in the light of God’s word, what obedience looks like there. Remove what feeds it where you can. Tell a trusted believer and ask him to ask you. When you fail, confess it at once, receive forgiveness, and go again the same day. Self-control is not gritted teeth alone; it is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:23), and it grows as you rely on him in specific, repeated choices.

On a Tuesday. Ask someone who knows you well which link they see missing in you, and then be specific: not I will be more loving, but I will visit, phone or help this person, whom I have been avoiding.

For worship. Look at the chain and see a portrait. Faith resting wholly on the Father, goodness without a stain, knowledge of the Father’s will so perfect that he did always what pleased him, self-control in the wilderness when he was hungry, steadfastness all the way to the cross, godliness that said not my will but yours, affection for his brothers, and love for his enemies. Every link was first in Christ. And the God who called us by that excellence has promised to reproduce it in us, giving lavishly what he asks us to supply lavishly, until the family likeness is complete.

verseByVerse.quote: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yours and increasing. Are yours, hyparchonta, means present in you; increasing, pleonazonta, means abounding. Peter assumes growth is the normal state, and that a static Christian life is already a warning sign. Living things grow. A tree that has not grown for years is either very old or dead.

Ineffective or unfruitful. Ineffective, argous, is literally idle, unemployed; it was used of land lying fallow and of the workers standing idle in the marketplace (Matthew 20:3, 6). Unfruitful, akarpous, is barren. Knowledge of Christ is meant to produce fruit (John 15:8; Colossians 1:10). Peter is not saying these qualities earn knowledge, but that without them a man’s knowing goes nowhere. You may hold the doctrine accurately and be entirely unproductive in it, like a field with the best soil in the county that nobody has sown.

So nearsighted that he is blind. The word, myōpazōn, from which comes myopic, means squinting, screwing up the eyes to see something close. The man can see what is right in front of him perfectly well, this week, this appetite, this grievance, this pay rise. What he cannot see is anything at a distance: eternity, the judgement seat, the coming kingdom, the souls of people around him. Short-sightedness, left alone, becomes blindness. And it is the false teachers’ disease exactly. They will scoff at the coming of the Lord (3:4), because they cannot see further than their own desires.

Having forgotten that he was cleansed. And there is the root. Forgotten is literally having taken forgetfulness (lēthēn labōn), as though he had picked it up and put it on. Cleansed, katharismos, is the word used of Christ’s work when he made purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3). He has lost sight of his own cleansing: not necessarily lost the cleansing, but the memory of it. A Christian who forgets what he was forgiven has no fuel for growth, because gratitude is the engine of the whole chain in verses 5–7. So when growth has stopped, look not usually for a missing technique, but for a memory that has gone dim. The woman in Luke 7 who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears loved much because she knew she had been forgiven much.

I feel stuck and fruitless. Am I a Christian at all? The fact that it troubles you is a good sign; the man Peter describes is not troubled, he is drowsy. Begin where Peter puts the problem: with memory. Go back to the cross and look again at what your sins cost and how freely they were washed away. Read a Gospel slowly, or Psalm 103, or Isaiah 53. Confess the specific sins that have choked growth. Then take one step of obedience in one of the qualities of verses 5–7. Fruit grows slowly and is often seen first by others, so ask a mature believer what they see. And do not judge your whole standing by one dry season; judge it by where you run.

On a Tuesday. Before you sleep tonight, lift your eyes past the next week: think about the day you will see Christ, and about one person you know who is without him. Then remember one specific sin you have been forgiven, and thank him for it by name. The memory will do more for your growth than a new resolution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be all the more diligent. Be diligent, spoudasate, echoes verse 5, and all the more raises it. And brothers is the only time in the letter Peter addresses his readers so. The warning about the blind man of verse 9 is followed at once by the warmth of family: a brother pleading with brothers.

To confirm your calling and election. The sentence has troubled readers, and the trouble dissolves on a careful look at who is being confirmed to whom. Confirm, bebaian poieisthai, means to make firm, make sure; a related word was a legal term for ratifying a contract or guaranteeing a sale. Calling is God’s effectual call; election, eklogē, is God’s eternal choice. Peter does not say make God’s election secure: that is not in anyone’s power, and this letter grounds everything in what God’s divine power has granted. Calling is mentioned first because it is how we come to know our election: we see the call in time and learn from it the choice made before time. We cannot make our election more certain to God; it is fixed. But we can make it more certain to ourselves, by growing in the qualities of verses 5–7, which are the evidence of genuine faith. The fruit does not create the root; it demonstrates it. That is how the Reformed tradition has generally read this: not works establishing salvation, but works establishing certainty.

The kindness in it. A Christian anxious about whether he is truly God’s is not told to search his memory for a decisive moment, nor to look inward for a feeling. He is told to look for growth in ordinary character, which is visible, and which other people can see too. Election is not a locked room to be broken into by speculation. It is a fact God has made known through his call, and confirmed in lives that are being changed.

You will never fall. Practise, poiountes, is present tense: keep doing. Never fall, ou mē ptaisēte pote, is a strong double negative: you will certainly never, ever stumble. James uses the verb of the many ways we all stumble in speech (James 3:2). Here it is not a promise of sinlessness but of not coming to ruin: you will never fall away, never be lost. We still stumble in lesser ways every day; but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his righteousness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and so our faltering practice is accepted for his sake.

Does if you practise these qualities mean that perseverance depends on our effort? The qualities are the fruit of the divine power that has given us all we need (v. 3), and by them believers confirm their calling, show it to be real, to themselves and others. Those who belong to Christ are kept by him (John 10:28–29); diligence is the way his keeping works out in our lives, not a rival to it.

Richly provided. Plousiōs epichorēgēthēsetai is the chorēgos word again, as in verse 5, and now the direction reverses. They were told to supply these qualities lavishly; God will lavishly supply their entrance. Entrance, eisodos, is a way in, a welcome: like a victorious general welcomed home through the city gates. Not a man scraping in as the door shuts, smelling of smoke (1 Corinthians 3:15), but a son coming home to a feast, into the kingdom no false teacher can scoff away.

Of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. The same construction as verse 1: one person, Lord and Saviour. The kingdom is his, and the way in is his doing. He entered once for all into the holy places, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12), and he told his disciples he was going to prepare a place for them and would come again to take them to himself (John 14:2–3). The entrance is richly provided because the King has already gone through the gate ahead of his people, and he is the one standing at it. Even the election Peter tells them to confirm was made in him, before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4).

Where Christians differ: can I know I am elect? Some fear election makes assurance impossible: how can I know if God chose me? Others think assurance comes only by special revelation. Verdict: Believers can and should have assurance of their election. It is grounded first in God’s promises in Christ, received by faith; it is confirmed by the Spirit’s inner witness (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit of a godly life (1 John 2:3; 3:14). Election is not a cause for anxiety but for confidence: those who trust Christ and grow in godliness may know they are chosen (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). And the elect will persevere: they will never fall.

Can a true Christian fall away and be lost? No. Those God has chosen and called he keeps, and none of them will be snatched out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6). True believers can fall into serious sin for a time, as Peter himself did on the night he denied the Lord, and they may lose the joy of their salvation and come under the Father’s discipline. But they are brought back, because Christ prays for them as he prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32). Those who abandon the faith altogether show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). Many faithful Christians in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, who hold that a believer can freely turn away and be lost, read the warnings of Scripture differently, and they rightly take those warnings seriously; this commentary holds the Reformed view of perseverance because of promises like John 10:28–29, while honouring them as brothers. So the promise of this verse is not a reason to relax but a reason to keep going without fear.

What if I look and cannot see the fruit? First, look at Christ before you look at yourself. Assurance rests first on his promise to receive all who come (John 6:37), not on your inspection. Second, look honestly but not morbidly: fruit is often small, slow and more visible to others than to you. Do you trust him? Do you want to obey him? Do you grieve over sin? Do you love his people? Third, if you find almost nothing, do not sit down in despair. Go to Christ now as a sinner, and begin to obey. The way to confirm your calling is not endless self-examination but present faith and diligence.

For worship. Before the world was made he chose us, and in time his voice found us and called us by name. He keeps those he calls, so that the one who stumbled on a dark night by a courtyard fire could write, half a lifetime later, you will never fall. The election was his, the calling was his, the keeping is his, and the welcome will be his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Facing the death Jesus foretold, Peter keeps reminding his readers of what they already know. Their faith rests on two witnesses that agree: the apostles who saw Christ’s majesty on the mountain, and the prophetic word, spoken by men whom the Holy Spirit carried along.
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried Along

Prophecy did not come from the prophet’s own interpretation. Men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along: fully human, and fully God’s word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote knowing his death was near, and arranged for his readers to remember.

Now: Scripture is a lamp in a dark place, enough light until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I intend always to remind you. Remind, hypomimnēskein, means keep reminding, and it is a key theme of the letter (1:12, 13, 15; 3:1–2). Peter is not correcting ignorance. He says plainly that they know these things, and he intends to go on saying them anyway. That cuts against the appetite for novelty the false teachers were exploiting. Most of what a congregation needs is not new information but the same truth said again, because knowing a thing and having it present to you are different states. A man knows he loves his wife; he still needs to remember it at six o’clock on a tiring evening.

Established in the truth. Established, estērigmenous, is perfect tense: settled and still standing. It is the word Jesus used to Peter on the night of the denial: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). The man who could not stand firm for a night is spending his last days making others firm.

As long as I am in this body. Body, skēnōma, is literally tent, and the image governs the paragraph. A tent is temporary accommodation, struck when the journey moves on (2 Corinthians 5:1–4). And stir you up, diegeirein, means to wake someone; it is used of the disciples waking Jesus in the storm (Luke 8:24), and Peter uses it again in 3:1. His model of ministry is not filling empty heads but waking drowsy ones. Perhaps he remembered Gethsemane, where three times he slept while his Lord prayed.

Is it not boring to hear the same things again and again? Only if you think the purpose of hearing is to collect information. Food is the same every day and nobody calls bread boring; we need it again because we used up the last meal. The gospel is like that. Yesterday’s assurance does not carry today’s temptation; the truth must be brought fresh to a heart that leaks. A good preacher will find new ways to say old things, but you should be suspicious of any teacher whose main selling point is that he has something nobody has heard before. In Christian truth, what is new is seldom true, and what is true is never stale to a hungry soul.

The putting off of my body. Apothesis is laying aside, as one takes off clothing or strikes a tent. Death is a laying aside of the body, not the end of the person. Peter speaks of it calmly, the way a traveller speaks of folding up his tent before the last stage of a journey.

As our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. Peter knows he is going to die because he was told. On the beach, after the third question about love, Jesus said that when he was old others would stretch out his hands and lead him where he did not want to go, and John adds that this indicated the kind of death by which he would glorify God (John 21:18–19). The church has long understood the stretched-out hands to mean crucifixion. Early tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero; a later tradition adds that he asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die as his Lord had. So this letter is written by a man under a sentence he has carried for most of his Christian life. He was told it on the morning of his restoration, in the same conversation in which Jesus said, follow me. And he has been following ever since, toward that death, with his eyes open.

After my departure. Departure, exodos, is the word Luke uses for what Moses and Elijah spoke of on the mountain: Jesus’ own death, his departure which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Peter had heard that conversation, and now uses the word of himself. His death is an exodus: a going out of bondage into the promised land, behind the Lord who went first. And what he does with the knowledge is striking. He is not settling affairs or saying farewells. He is arranging for them to remember after he has gone. He may mean this letter itself, or perhaps Mark’s Gospel, which early tradition says records Peter’s preaching.

How should a Christian think about his own death? As Peter did: as the folding of a tent and an exodus, not as the end. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), at once, not in a sleep and not in a purgatory, but with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). We may still fear dying, the process, the pain, the parting, and that is no sin; even Jesus was in anguish in the garden. But death itself has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). So use the time well. Peter’s question was not how long have I left? but what will they remember when I am gone? Ask the same.

On a Tuesday. Who will remember Christ better because of you: your children, a younger believer, a friend? A few lines telling one of them what Christ has been to you may outlast much else you leave, and you need not be dying to write them.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had told Peter how he would die.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not cleverly devised myths. Cleverly devised, sesophismenois, means cunningly crafted, made up. The false teachers were evidently saying that the promised coming of Christ was a story, the kind of tale religious men tell to frighten people into good behaviour. Peter’s reply is not philosophical but historical. The ancient world was full of myths: stories of gods and heroes set in a distant, timeless past, which no one could date or check. The gospel is not like that. It names a governor, a city, a mountain, and men who were there.

The power and coming. Dynamin kai parousian probably means his powerful coming: the second coming, which the false teachers denied (3:4). Parousia was used of the arrival of a king on a state visit. The apostles did not invent the return of Christ. They had already seen a preview of it.

Eyewitnesses of his majesty. The word for eyewitnesses, epoptai, was used in the mystery religions for those admitted to the highest grade of initiation: those who had seen. Peter takes a word from the cults, with their secret rites and private visions, and applies it to something that happened on a mountain in daylight before three fishermen. Majesty, megaleiotēs, is the word used when the crowds were astonished at the majesty of God in Jesus’ healing (Luke 9:43). At the Transfiguration, Peter saw the King’s face as it will be seen on the day he comes.

Honor and glory from God the Father. Peter is describing the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36), and he was one of three men there: the honour of the Father’s word, and the glory of the Son’s own radiance shining through.

The Majestic Glory. A reverent way of naming God, perhaps referring to the bright cloud of God’s presence that overshadowed them. If so, it is the cloud that filled the tabernacle and the temple, the glory that Moses asked to see, come down again on the mountain. Matthew tells us that when the disciples heard the voice they fell on their faces, terrified (Matthew 17:6). Holiness that near is not cosy. Then Jesus came and touched them and told them to rise and not be afraid (Matthew 17:7): the glory that flattens sinners belongs to the one who lifts them up.

My beloved Son. The Father’s declaration echoes Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1, and the words at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17). Look at what Peter selects. He does not describe the shining face or the white clothes or Moses and Elijah. He reports the voice, because the argument concerns testimony, and what settles the matter is not what he saw but what was said. The Father himself named his Son, King and Servant, and declared his delight in him.

On the holy mountain. The emphasis is on hearing, twice, and on presence. The mountain was made holy by God’s presence as Sinai once was; tradition suggests Mount Tabor, though Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, fits the Gospel accounts well. And there is something moving in the restraint. Peter had wanted to build three shelters and stay, and had spoken without knowing what he was saying (Luke 9:33). He mentions none of that. Decades on he reports only what is admissible: we were there, and we heard.

Why does the Transfiguration prove that Christ will come again? Because it was the coming in miniature. Jesus had just said that some standing there would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28), and six days later three of them did: the glory he will have when he comes was briefly uncovered before their eyes. The scoffers said the King would never come in power. Peter replies that he has already seen the King in his power. What was hidden for a moment on the mountain will be revealed to the whole world on the last day.

How do we know the apostles were not simply mistaken or lying? Consider what their testimony cost them. Men do not willingly die for what they know to be a lie, and Peter is writing under the shadow of crucifixion. Sincerity alone does not prove a thing true, but these men were not reporting a private belief: they claimed to have seen and heard for themselves, so they were in a position to know whether it was a lie. Some scholars think this letter was written by a follower after Peter’s death; even so, the Transfiguration does not rest on this letter alone, for three Gospels report it, written within living memory. Their accounts are sober, full of their own failures, written within living memory of the events, when others who were there could contradict them. And the testimony is not one man’s vision: three men on the mountain, and hundreds who saw the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:6). Christian faith is not a leap in the dark; it is trust in reliable witnesses, confirmed by the Spirit who opens our eyes to see that what they say is true.

Should I seek experiences of glory like Peter’s? No. Peter himself, having had the greatest experience a man could have, does not tell his readers to seek one. He points them in the next verse to the prophetic word. The Transfiguration was a unique moment given to chosen witnesses to found the church’s testimony, and it has been written down so that you may believe without seeing (John 20:29). God may give believers deep joy and a sense of his nearness, and we may thank him for it, but our faith rests on what happened and what is written, not on what we feel.

On a Tuesday. When someone dismisses the faith as a nice story, do not be rattled or defensive. Say plainly that Christianity stands or falls on events, a death and a resurrection witnessed by named men, and offer to read one of the Gospels with them.
verseByVerse.note: The “holy mountain” is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus’ glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophetic word more fully confirmed. The prophetic word is the Old Testament Scriptures as a whole, which prophesy Christ, including his coming in glory. More fully confirmed, bebaioteron, is from the same family as the word for confirming your calling (v. 10). There are two readings. First, the Transfiguration confirmed the prophecies, making them even more certain to us: the voice on the mountain and the writings agree. Second, the prophetic Scriptures are even more reliable than Peter’s experience. The second fits well with verses 20–21: Scripture is more certain than any experience, even an apostle’s vision, because it comes from God himself. Either way Peter is not belittling what he saw; he has just staked his case on being an eyewitness. And either way his readers, who were not on the mountain and never would be, are told that what they hold in their hands is the firmest ground there is.

Is Scripture really more certain than seeing something with my own eyes? Yes, in this sense: eyes can be deceived, memories fade, and experiences need interpreting, but God’s written word does not change and cannot lie. Peter’s experience on the mountain was real, yet it lasted minutes, was seen by three men, and needed words from God to explain it. Scripture is God’s own permanent testimony, given for every believer in every age. So when an experience, a dream, an impression or a strong feeling seems to say one thing and Scripture says another, Scripture wins every time. That is not distrust of God’s work in us; it is trust in his clearest word to us.

You will do well to pay attention. Pay attention, prosechontes, means hold the mind on, as a sailor holds his eye on a light. And you will do well is gentle: not a threat but the encouragement of a guide.

A lamp shining in a dark place. The image is exactly weighted. Lamp, lychnos, is a small oil lamp. Dark place, auchmēros topos, means a dry, dirty, murky place, the kind of corner where nothing grows and nobody would choose to stay. This world, darkened by sin and false teaching, is like that room, and Scripture is the lamp that shows the way (Psalm 119:105). A lamp is not the sun; it is enough to see the next few feet by, and it is indispensable if the alternative is total darkness. Peter is honest about how much light Scripture gives in this age: sufficient, and not yet daylight. We do not see everything. We see enough to walk.

Until the day dawns. Literally shines through: the day of Christ’s return (Romans 13:12), when the night of this age is over. The lamp is temporary. There is a morning coming, and when it arrives nobody will need a lamp.

The morning star. Phōsphoros, light-bearer, is the planet Venus, the last light before sunrise and the herald of it. It points to Christ himself, the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16), the star that would come out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17), the sun of righteousness who rises with healing in his wings (Malachi 4:2). So the dawn is his coming, which is precisely what the false teachers were denying. In your hearts is the phrase that surprises. Peter has been arguing about history and testimony, and lands on the inward. When Christ returns, believers will know him fully (1 Corinthians 13:12). The same Christ who will appear publicly is the one who will fill the heart with light. Until then, we need the lamp of Scripture.

Does God still speak today apart from the Bible? This commentary holds that the gifts of new revelation, prophecy in the sense of authoritative words from God, ceased with the apostles, and that the canon of Scripture is closed (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). The reason is that the apostles and prophets were the church’s foundation, laid once (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is not laid again in every generation. Many dear brothers in Christ believe otherwise, and we hold our view with charity. But on the practical point there is wide agreement among Bible-believing Christians: Scripture is the lamp, sufficient for faith and life, and nothing that claims to be from God may add to it or contradict it. The Spirit does speak today, through the word he inspired, applying it to our hearts. If you want to hear God speak, open the Bible.

On a Tuesday. Before a decision, a hard conversation or a temptation today, read a passage and hold your mind on it. And if you have let the lamp gather dust, light it again tonight with a chapter of a Gospel, asking the Lord to show you himself in it.

For worship. God has not left us in the dark. He lit a lamp and put it in our hands, and every page of it was shining toward one Person. The prophets saw his star rising from far off; the apostles saw his glory on the mountain; and we hold their word, more sure than any vision. One day the lamp will be set down, not because it failed, but because the Sun himself has come, and we shall see him whom we have loved without seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing this first of all. Above all, of first importance: before anything else about Scripture, know where it came from.

Someone’s own interpretation. The verse is quoted in two directions, and the context settles it. Interpretation, epilysis, means explanation, the solving of something obscure. It is often taken to mean that no individual may interpret Scripture privately. That may be a reasonable caution, but it is not what Peter is arguing here. The subject throughout is the origin of prophecy, not its later handling, and verse 21 explains verse 20 directly, beginning with for. Prophecy did not arise from the prophet’s own reading of things. It was not a gifted man’s insight into his times. The message came from outside the prophet, from God.

Never produced by the will of man. Produced, ēnechthē, means was brought, was carried. The negative is absolute. Scripture did not begin with human initiative or decision. No prophet sat down and decided to write the word of God.

Men spoke from God. Two things held together, and the New Testament’s doctrine of Scripture lives in the combination. Men spoke: real people, with their own vocabulary, style and circumstances. Isaiah does not sound like Amos; Paul does not sound like John. (The KJV’s holy men of God spake follows later manuscripts; the earliest read men spoke from God, as most modern Bibles do.) And they spoke from God: the message originated with him.

Carried along by the Holy Spirit. The verb, pheromenoi, is a sailing word. It is used in Acts 27:15 and 17 of Paul’s ship, which had lost the power to steer and was driven before the wind. And it is the same verb Peter used twice in verses 17–18 of the voice borne from heaven. The voice was carried to the mountain; the prophets were carried by the Spirit. The men are not passive cargo; they are working the vessel, raising the sails. But the Spirit supplied the power and direction, and they arrived where the wind took them. This is the doctrine of inspiration: Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), fully human and fully divine in its authorship, so that what Scripture says, God says. That is why Peter can appeal to it against men who were rewriting the future to suit themselves. And that is what is meant by calling Scripture inerrant: because God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19), whatever Scripture affirms is true, in its history as much as in its doctrine.

The Spirit of Christ in them. Peter had already said who the Spirit carrying the prophets was, and what he was carrying them toward. In his first letter he wrote that the Spirit of Christ in the prophets was indicating the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1 Peter 1:11). The wind that drove the prophetic ship blew from Christ and toward Christ. And Peter had learned to read the Scriptures that way from Christ himself, who on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and who said plainly that Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). The Christian receives the Bible as the Lord Jesus received it: every word from God, and every page about him.

In the flow. Verses 20–21 finish the answer Peter began in verse 16. The message of Christ’s coming is no myth, first because the apostles saw his majesty (vv. 16–18), and second because the prophets spoke from God (vv. 19–21). They also open the next chapter, which begins, But false prophets also arose among the people (2:1). The contrast is deliberate: the true prophets were carried along by the Spirit; the false teachers are driven by their own greed and desires (2:3, 10). And chapter 3 will ask the readers to remember the words of these holy prophets (3:2), so this sentence about where Scripture comes from lies under the whole letter.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture fully inspired and without error? Some hold that Scripture is inspired only in its religious teaching, or that it contains human errors alongside divine truth. Verdict: Because Scripture came from God through men carried along by the Spirit, it shares God’s truthfulness. It is inerrant in all that it affirms, infallible in its teaching, and sufficient for faith and life. The human authors were not mere typewriters; God used their personalities and research (Luke 1:1–4). But the Spirit so guided them that what they wrote is the very word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Sola Scriptura: Scripture is the final authority over every tradition, experience and claim of revelation.

Does this mean that individual Christians may not interpret Scripture for themselves? Roman Catholic teaching has used the verse to argue that the church alone can interpret Scripture rightly. But Peter is speaking of where prophecy came from: not from the prophet’s own understanding, but from God, as men were carried along by the Spirit (v. 21). Every believer is to read and understand Scripture (Acts 17:11), humbly, in the fellowship of the church and with its teachers, testing all interpretation by Scripture itself.

Does this apply to the New Testament too? Yes. Peter speaks here of Old Testament prophecy, but in 3:2 he puts the commandment of the apostles alongside the prophets, and in 3:15–16 he places Paul’s letters among the other Scriptures. The same Spirit who carried the prophets was promised to the apostles to bring to their remembrance all that Jesus said and to guide them into all the truth (John 14:26; 16:13). The church did not make these books Scripture; it recognised the voice of its Shepherd in them. With the apostles’ writings the canon is complete, and no further book will be added (Jude 3; Hebrews 1:1–2).

What about the parts of the Bible that seem to contradict each other or science? Take them seriously, but humbly. Many apparent contradictions dissolve when we read carefully: different writers choosing different details, round numbers, the way ancient historians summarised speeches, or ordinary language describing what the eye sees, as we still say the sun rises. Some difficulties remain unsolved, and good Christian scholars have honestly said so. But a difficulty is not an error, and a great many supposed errors of a century ago have since been answered. When you meet one, keep reading, ask a mature teacher, consult a good commentary, and trust the God who cannot lie (Titus 1:2).

On a Tuesday. Before you open Scripture today, ask the Spirit who carried its writers to open your eyes. And when the word rebukes you, do not argue with the wind; set your sails by it.

1.theology:
The chapter’s great claim is that believers become partakers of the divine nature (v. 4). This is not deification in the sense of becoming God or merging into his being. It is moral sharing: through the Spirit and union with Christ, God’s own character, his holiness, patience, love and truthfulness, is formed in the believer. Calvin read it as a sharing in God’s qualities, not in his essence. Sanctification is this sharing worked out in ordinary virtue.

The doctrine of Scripture (vv. 20–21) is equally central. Scripture is God’s own word spoken through human writers whom the Spirit carried along, so their words carry his authority. That is why the prophetic word is more fully confirmed: the written word outlasts the eyewitness and is open to every believer.
1.examples:
The chain of virtues (vv. 5–7) speaks to Christians who stop at faith and see no need to grow. Peter’s answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. The virtues are not the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence that it is real and the direction of its growth.

The lamp (v. 19) helps believers who find Bible reading dry. You do not read it because it is always exciting; you read it because you are in a dark place and it is the lamp God has given. The darkness is no reason to put the lamp down.

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: <sup>1</sup>But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.<sup>2</sup>And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.<sup>3</sup>And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.<sup>4</sup>For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment;<sup>5</sup>if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly;<sup>6</sup>if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;<sup>7</sup>and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked<sup>8</sup>(for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard);<sup>9</sup>then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,<sup>10</sup>and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones,<sup>11</sup>whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.<sup>12</sup>But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction,<sup>13</sup>suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you.<sup>14</sup>They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!<sup>15</sup>Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing,<sup>16</sup>but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.<sup>17</sup>These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved.<sup>18</sup>For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error.<sup>19</sup>They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.<sup>20</sup>For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.<sup>21</sup>For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.<sup>22</sup>What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Peter’s portrait of the false teacher: his method (slipping in quietly), his doctrine (denying the Master), his motive (greed) and his end (judgment already on its way). Three examples from history, the angels, the flood and Sodom, show that God judges the wicked and rescues the godly. Then Peter describes the teachers themselves: arrogant, driven by appetite, greedy like Balaam, preying on new believers.

The key irony is v. 19: they promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. The test of a teacher is not the sophistication of his words but the shape of his life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: False prophets troubled Israel, and false teachers will trouble the church. They bring in destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, and exploit people for money. But history shows how God acts: he did not spare the angels who sinned, the ancient world, or Sodom, yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the wicked for judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
Righteous Lot

False teachers arise from within. God did not spare the angels, the ancient world or Sodom, yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. He knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Lot, compromised as he was, was tormented by the evil he saw day after day.

Now: Being grieved by the world’s evil is a mark of the righteous; being comfortable with it is the danger.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Peter 2 is a sustained warning against false teachers. As Israel had false prophets, the church will have false teachers, who smuggle in destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, lead many into immorality and exploit believers out of greed; their judgement is certain (vv. 1–3). Three judgements prove it, the angels who sinned, the world of Noah’s day, and Sodom, and two rescues, Noah and Lot: the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unrighteous for judgement (vv. 4–9). The teachers indulge the flesh, despise authority, have eyes full of adultery and hearts trained in greed, and follow Balaam (vv. 10–16). They are waterless springs, promising freedom while slaves of corruption (vv. 17–19). Having escaped the world’s defilements through knowing Christ, they are entangled again, like a dog returning to its vomit or a washed sow to the mud (vv. 20–22).

The setting. Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude. Most scholars think 2 Peter drew on Jude, though some think Jude drew on 2 Peter, or both on common material; nothing in the meaning depends on which. The false teachers seem to have combined a denial of Christ’s return and future judgement (3:3–4) with moral licence: since there is no judgement coming, live as you please. They may have twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into permission to sin (3:15–16). Peter has just spoken of the true prophets, carried along by the Spirit (1:21). Now he turns to the counterfeit, and the hinge is the word but.

False prophets also arose. In Israel’s history many claimed to speak for God but did not (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:9–40). Every true prophet had his shadow. Moses had Balaam, Elijah had the prophets of Baal, Micaiah had four hundred court prophets promising the king victory, Jeremiah had Hananiah, who broke the yoke off the prophet’s neck and promised freedom within two years (Jeremiah 28:10–11), and a crowd of prophets crying peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Israel had them; the church will have them. Nobody should be surprised.

False teachers among you. Among comes twice: among the people, among you. Inside the church, not outside (Acts 20:29–30; Matthew 7:15), which is what makes them dangerous and hard to name. A persecutor is easy to recognise. A false teacher sits in the next pew, sings the same hymns, and uses the same vocabulary.

Secretly bring in destructive heresies. Pareisaxousin means to smuggle in, to slip in alongside. Nothing is announced. Error rarely arrives as a replacement for the truth. It arrives as an addition, placed beside it, until one day the truth has been edged out of the room. Heresies, haireseis, originally meant choices, then factions, and later false teachings that destroy the faith: a man’s own preference set up against what was delivered.

Denying the Master who bought them. Denying, arnoumenoi, is disowning, by their teaching and their lives (Titus 1:16; Jude 4). The word is painful on Peter’s lips: it is the word used of his own three denials in the courtyard. He knows what it is to deny the Lord, and what it is to be brought back. These men deny him and have no tears. Master, despotēs, is sovereign lord, the owner of slaves. Bought, agorasanta, is the slave-market word, the language of redemption (1 Corinthians 6:20; Revelation 5:9). The picture is of purchased slaves repudiating the man who paid for them, and their destruction, swift and sudden, is one they bring upon themselves.

Where Christians differ: does “the Master who bought them” prove Christ died for everyone, including those who perish? Arminians (Christians who hold that Christ died to make salvation possible for everyone, with each person’s free response deciding the outcome) and some others, including some Calvinists, cite this verse to argue that Christ paid for the sins of all, including false teachers who are finally lost. The Reformed view, often called definite or particular atonement, is that Christ died to secure the salvation of his people. Godly believers have long differed here, and the debate is about how wide Christ’s purpose was, not about whether his death is offered freely to all. Verdict: Several points apply. The word is Master (despotēs), not Saviour or Redeemer; it pictures a slave-owner who has purchased slaves, and the false teachers deny his rightful ownership. Peter may be speaking of their own profession: they claimed to be bought by Christ and part of the church, and Peter describes them according to that profession, as one might speak of a church member. Or he may be echoing Deuteronomy 32:6, where Israel as a nation is said to have been bought by God, though many Israelites were not saved. The verse does not use the language of effective redemption from sin (as in 1 Peter 1:18–19). Scripture elsewhere teaches that Christ laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), that his death actually secures the salvation of those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; Hebrews 10:14), and that the sheep are never lost (John 10:28). The best reading is that the false teachers professed to belong to the Master who purchased the church, and their denial exposed that profession as false.

Were these men ever saved? The chapter suggests not. They returned to their old ways like a dog to its vomit (v. 22), showing that their nature had never changed. They stood within the covenant community and enjoyed everything that came with it: the preaching, the fellowship, the table, the outward cleansing of a changed reputation. And they turned on the One who purchased the church. Peter is not writing a treatise on the extent of the atonement; he is using the language of ownership to make the ingratitude vivid. The lesson for us is not to puzzle over their secret state but to examine our own: do I merely belong to a church that Christ bought, or do I belong to Christ?

Many will follow their sensuality. Sensuality, aselgeia, is unrestrained immorality, shameless excess. And it is many who follow. False teaching is popular, because it usually offers what the flesh already wants; false living then looks for teaching that will excuse it. So the question is not only who is teaching error but why we might want to hear it. A teacher who promises comfort, success or freedom from rebuke is selling to an appetite already in the room, and Paul warned that people would gather teachers to suit their own passions (2 Timothy 4:3).

The way of truth will be blasphemed. The way of truth is Christianity, the way (Acts 9:2). That is the real damage: the gospel’s reputation suffers. Outsiders judge the way of truth by the people carrying its name (Romans 2:24), and this letter’s readers were already being slandered (1 Peter 2:12).

In their greed they will exploit you. Greed, pleonexia, is the craving for more, as in 1 Timothy 6:5. Exploit, emporeusontai, is a trading word, from which comes emporium: they will make merchandise of you. The congregation is the commodity. False words, plastois logois, are moulded words, from which comes plastic: words shaped to sell rather than to tell the truth.

Not idle, not asleep. From long ago God has pronounced judgement on such people (Jude 4). Not idle, ouk argei, is the same root as the ineffective Christian of 1:8; not asleep, ou nystazei, is the word used of the virgins who all grew drowsy (Matthew 25:5). Both images personify judgement as something awake and moving. It has been on its way for a long time and has not stopped.

How can I tell a false teacher from a true one who makes mistakes? Look at three things Peter names. First, what he does with Christ: does he deny the Master, his deity, his lordship, his atoning death, his return, or does he exalt him? Second, his life: is his teaching producing holiness or licence, in him and in those who follow him? Third, his motive: is he serving the flock or using it, for money, power or admiration? A sincere teacher may be wrong on secondary matters and still love Christ, live humbly and feed the sheep. Treat him as a brother. A teacher who denies Christ, excuses sin and enriches himself is what this chapter describes, however gifted.

What should I do if I suspect false teaching in my church? Do not gossip and do not panic. First test what is taught by Scripture, carefully and fairly (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). If you are still concerned, speak privately to the person, or to your elders, who are charged with guarding the flock (Acts 20:28–31; Titus 1:9). Be specific about what was said and why it troubles you. If the elders themselves are teaching what denies the gospel and will not be corrected, you may need to leave for a faithful church, quietly and without bitterness.
