Pray for those being misled, and keep your own heart close to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every theological disagreement is a destructive heresy. Peter is speaking of denying Christ, combined with immoral living and greed.

On a Tuesday. Test the teachers you listen to online and the books on your nightstand, not only the pulpit. Ask of each one: does this make Christ greater to me, and make me holier and more generous, or does it make me more comfortable with myself?

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God did not spare angels. Peter now argues from history, and the sentence is a single long conditional running from verse 4 to verse 9: if, if, if, then. Three examples of judgement, and woven among them, two of rescue. Did not spare, ouk epheisato, is the verb Paul uses of God not sparing his own Son (Romans 8:32), and it is worth holding the two together. God did not spare the angels who sinned, because they deserved judgement. He did not spare his Son, who did not, so that he might spare us. The first case is the highest of creatures: if rank protected anybody it would have protected them, and it did not.

Cast them into hell. Hell here is Tartarus (tartarōsas), used only here in the New Testament: a term from Greek thought for the deepest place of confinement, lower than Hades. Peter borrows a term his readers would understand, as he borrowed the mystery-cult word for eyewitnesses in 1:16.

Chains of gloomy darkness. Chains, seirais; some manuscripts read sirois, pits. Gloomy darkness, zophos, is the darkness of the underworld. Kept, tēroumenous, is held in custody: custody rather than sentence. They are held for a trial that has not yet happened (Jude 6; Revelation 20:10). Not all demons are bound, since many are active (Ephesians 6:12); these particular angels are.

Which angels are these? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan at the beginning. Others, following Jewish tradition, link them with the sons of God who sinned with human women before the flood (Genesis 6:1–4), as Jude 6–7 may also do; and the order here (angels, then the flood, then Sodom) follows Genesis, which suggests the Genesis 6 sin. Calvin and many Reformed writers read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as the godly line of Seth instead. Peter does not stop to settle it; the angel reading is the more likely one, held here without dogmatism. What is plain is that angels sinned, are now held for judgement, and will be judged. And the point stands either way: if God did not spare angels, he will not spare false teachers.

The ancient world. The second example: the flood (Genesis 6–8). Not one city now, but the whole world except one family.

But preserved Noah. The second case adds the note that will govern the whole argument: God did not merely judge, he preserved. Herald of righteousness, dikaiosynēs kēryx, is a preacher of righteousness. Genesis records no sermon of Noah’s, but Jewish tradition held that he warned his generation, and Peter, by inspiration, confirms it. We may understand the building of the ark itself as a proclamation: years of hammering in the sight of neighbours who thought him mad, every plank a sermon about a coming flood. With seven others is literally the eighth: Noah, his wife, three sons and their wives. Peter counts the survivors, as in 1 Peter 3:20. Faithfulness is not measured by numbers.

The world of the ungodly. Ungodly, asebōn, means without regard for God. The world of Noah’s day was not irreligious in the sense of having no gods; it simply lived as though the true God did not matter. Jesus said they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark (Matthew 24:38).

Sodom and Gomorrah. The third example (Genesis 19), and the most public. Their sins included sexual immorality and violence (Genesis 19:4–9; Jude 7), and also pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50). So the three build: the highest creatures, the whole world, and the most notorious cities. If none of those was spared, the case Peter is making does not need arguing further.

An example. Hypodeigma is a pattern set out for others to look at, a warning. The desolate country by the Dead Sea, where the cities were remembered to have stood, functioned that way in Jewish memory for centuries. Past judgements are previews of the final judgement (Luke 17:26–30).

Is it not harsh to talk about judgement like this? It would be harsh only if it were untrue, or if it were said without tears. God’s judgement is not a flaw in his love but the expression of his holiness and justice; a God who never judged evil would not be good. And look how Peter tells it: in every case judgement is accompanied by rescue, and it comes after long patience. God waited while Noah built; he would have spared Sodom for ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). Speaking of judgement is a kindness when it moves people to flee to Christ, who bore it in their place. The cruel thing would be to stay silent.

On a Tuesday. If you feel foolish for believing in a coming day while everyone else carries on as normal, think of Noah’s hammer. He looked foolish for a long time. Then it rained.

For worship. The Lord shut Noah in with his own hand, and then the rain came. Outside the ark the waters were judgement; inside, the same waters lifted eight people above a drowned world and set them down on a washed earth. Jesus called his death a baptism he had to undergo (Luke 12:50), and the flood of judgement went over him; those who are in him are carried through it into a new creation, saved through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 3:21). He has never lost one soul that he shut in.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here is Tartarus, a Greek term for the deepest place of punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteous Lot. This is the surprise of the paragraph, because Genesis does not present Lot flatteringly. He chose the well-watered plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:10–13); he offered his daughters to the mob (19:8); he lingered when the angels told him to flee, and had to be dragged out by the hand (19:16); and the story of his family afterwards is squalid (19:30–38). Yet Peter calls him righteous three times in two verses. It is not sentimentality. Lot was righteous by faith, as Abraham was, and God rescued him (Genesis 19:15–16, 29). It is the New Testament’s settled way of describing people who belong to God: not on the basis of their record but of their standing. If Lot is righteous, the word cannot mean impressive. Rescued, errysato, is the word in the Lord’s Prayer: deliver us from evil.

Greatly distressed. Kataponoumenon means worn down, oppressed, exhausted. Wicked, athesmōn, is lawless. Here is the evidence Peter goes on, and it is entirely inward. Lot did very little; what he did was suffer.

Tormenting his righteous soul. Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did protest the men’s demands (Genesis 19:7). Peter, by inspiration, reveals what Lot felt. Tormenting, ebasanizen, is a strong verb: the word for testing metal on a touchstone and for torment under interrogation. And day after day names the form it took: not one crisis but daily attrition, a man who had chosen to live there and could not stop being grieved by it. What he saw and heard got into him. Believers today should likewise be grieved, not entertained, by the wickedness around them.

A comfort for the compromised. This is a genuine encouragement to a believer who has made poor choices and is living in their consequences. If the mark of a righteous man in Sodom is that the place still distresses him, then the reader who feels worn down by the world around him has evidence rather than condemnation. The people who are comfortable are the ones in danger. And God rescued Lot even though he lingered: the angels seized him by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him (Genesis 19:16).

The Lord knows how to rescue. Here is the conclusion of the long sentence (vv. 4–9), and both halves matter. Knows how, oiden: he has the wisdom and the power, and the readers do not have to work out the mechanism. Godly, eusebeis, is the word of 1:3, 6, 7; trials, peirasmos, the same word as in 1 Peter 1:6. He found a boat for one and a road out of the city for the other. He knows how.

Rescued from the present evil age. Lot’s rescue is a small picture of a greater one. Angels went into Sodom to bring one man out; the Son of God came into this world itself, and did not merely take us by the hand but gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age (Galatians 1:4). And the verdict righteous, spoken over a man with Lot’s record, has only one explanation: God justifies the ungodly for the sake of another, the righteous one who suffered for the unrighteous (Romans 4:5; 1 Peter 3:18). To justify means to declare in the right: God the Judge pronounces a guilty man righteous, not because his record is clean, but because the record of Christ is counted as his. The Lord knows how to rescue, and at the cross he showed how.

To keep the unrighteous under punishment. Keep, tērein, is the custody word of verse 4. The same providence does both: rescuing and keeping are one skill, not two. Under punishment, kolazomenous, is a present participle: being punished. The wicked who have died are already experiencing punishment, held for the final judgement (Luke 16:23–24). Some translations take the participle as looking ahead, to be punished at the judgement, but the present tense most naturally means punishment already under way. On that reading this supports a conscious intermediate state for the wicked as well as for the righteous: there is no soul sleep, and the dead are not unconscious until the last day. And it is real punishment, not purification: there is no purgatory here, only custody until the judgement.

What if I live, like Lot, somewhere I chose badly? First, take comfort: God did not abandon Lot, and he will not abandon you. Second, take warning: Lot lost much in Sodom: his possessions, his sons-in-law, his wife, and his daughters’ moral compass, and you can lose a great deal by staying where you are drawn into sin. Ask honestly whether your work, neighbourhood, friendships or entertainment are wearing down your love for God or merely wearing you down with grief. If the first, seek a way out, as God may be providing one. If the second, stay faithful, keep praying, and let your grief become prayer for the people around you.

How can I be grieved by the world without becoming bitter or self-righteous? Remember that Lot’s grief came from love of righteousness, not contempt for people. Grieve over sin as one who has been forgiven much, not as one who is better. Pray for those whose deeds trouble you, that God would turn them from their ways. Speak truth gently when you can. And turn your distress toward God, not toward endless complaining about the culture; Lot’s torment was in his soul before the Lord. A heart grieved by sin and full of mercy for sinners looks like Christ, who wept over Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will always be rescued from suffering in this life. It means God will finally rescue them, through death if necessary, and will never abandon them.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did call the men’s intent wicked (Gen 19:7); Peter draws out the inner side of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The Portrait, and the Washed Sow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter now describes the teachers themselves: reckless toward spiritual powers, driven by appetite, greedy like Balaam, preying on new believers with promises of freedom. Having known the way of righteousness and turned back, they are worse off than before.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed, Not Changed

The false teachers promise freedom while slaves of corruption. The washed sow returns to the mire because her nature was never changed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Like Balaam, they loved gain and preyed on unsteady new believers.

Now: The question is not whether you have been washed, but whether you have been changed.

verseByVerse.quote: and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Defiling passion. Peter turns from the examples to the men themselves, and two marks come first. Indulge, poreuomenous, is literally walk after: their desires lead and they follow. Defiling passion, epithymia miasmou, is polluting lust, sexual immorality of various kinds. The first mark is appetite.

And despise authority. Authority, kyriotēs, is lordship: either Christ’s lordship, or church authority, or angelic powers. That is the second mark, and the one Peter develops. These men will not be told anything by anybody. And the two marks belong together: a man who wants to follow his appetites must first get rid of anyone who has the right to say no.

Bold and willful. Bold, tolmētai, is reckless. Willful, authadeis, is self-pleasing, stubborn, as in Titus 1:7, where an elder must not be so. Together they describe a confidence with no external check on it, which is exactly what makes a false teacher persuasive. Uncertain people are drawn to certainty, and these men never doubt themselves.

The glorious ones. Doxas, glories, are angelic beings, probably fallen angels or demons. The false teachers speak contemptuously of evil spirits, perhaps claiming that their freedom made them invulnerable. The point is not only what they said but the ease with which they said it, as men who have never considered that the unseen world might be real.

Whereas angels. Then the comparison, and it cuts deep. Even holy angels, who actually know what these powers are, who are far stronger, and who outrank the men entirely, do not insult evil spirits but leave judgement to God. Jude 9 gives the example of the archangel Michael, in a story not told in the Old Testament but known from Jewish tradition, who, disputing with the devil over Moses’ body, did not rebuke him himself but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” So the contrast is between beings who have seen the reality and are careful, and men who have seen nothing and are careless. Ignorance is producing the confidence.

The lordship they despise. The lordship these men wave away is most naturally the Lord’s own. They have already been described as denying the Master who bought them (v. 1), and in the parallel passage Jude says the same men reject authority (Jude 8). That is what makes their boldness so blind. The one whose lordship they despise is the one before whom an unclean spirit cried out in the synagogue at Capernaum, I know who you are, the Holy One of God, and was silenced with a word (Mark 1:24–25). Michael would not pronounce judgement on the devil because judgement belongs to the Lord, and the Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22). The men who joke about the powers are joking in front of their Judge.

A lesson in reverence. A settled reverence about what one does not understand is a mark of spiritual maturity, and a readiness to talk loosely about the unseen is usually a sign of having thought about it very little. The same is true of the holy things of God: the man who jokes easily about judgement, hell or the devil has rarely looked at them long.

How should a Christian deal with the devil, then? Firmly, humbly, and in Christ’s name, not our own. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9; James 4:7). Put on the armour of God, which is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation and the word (Ephesians 6:10–18). Pray. Flee temptation. You do not need to shout at demons, mock them, or seek them out; Michael simply appealed to the Lord. Nor do you need to fear them: greater is he who is in you (1 John 4:4). The posture is quiet confidence in Christ’s victory, not bravado and not terror.

What about authority I genuinely disagree with? Despising authority is not the same as disagreeing with it. You may question a decision, appeal respectfully, or, where an authority commands sin, obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Where authority is abused, especially in cases of abuse of the vulnerable, it must be exposed and the victims protected; that is not rebellion but righteousness. What Peter condemns is the settled heart that refuses to be under anyone, God included, so that it can do as it pleases.

verseByVerse.quote: But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like irrational animals. Irrational, aloga, is the word logos negated: without reason. The comparison is not merely abusive; it is diagnostic. An animal acts on appetite without deliberation, and Peter says that is precisely how these men operate. They have exchanged reason for instinct, which is why arguing with them achieves nothing. And there is a sad irony set against chapter 1: believers were made partakers of the divine nature; these men have sunk to the merely natural.

Born to be caught and destroyed. Like wild animals that end in hunters’ traps, men who live by appetite follow their nose to the bait and never see the snare. They speak loudest about what they understand least, and they will perish in their perishing: the ruin they bring on others is the ruin they receive.

Suffering wrong as the wage. Another wordplay: adikoumenoi misthon adikias, being wronged as the wage of wrong. They wanted wages; they will get them. And the word for wage prepares for Balaam in verse 15.

To revel in the daytime. Revel, tryphē, is luxurious indulgence. Even by the standards of a Greek city, serious drinking belonged to the night; Paul says those who get drunk are drunk at night (1 Thessalonians 5:7). These people indulge shamelessly in broad daylight. Shame has gone.

Blots and blemishes. Blots, spiloi, are stains; blemishes, mōmoi, defects. This is a deliberate reversal. Believers were ransomed with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19), and in 3:14 Peter will urge them to be found without spot or blemish. The spotless Lamb died to have a spotless people (Ephesians 5:25–27). And here are blemished men sitting at the very meals where the church remembered the unblemished Lamb, parodying everything his death was meant to produce.

While they feast with you. There is the sting. Deceptions, apatais; some manuscripts read agapais, love feasts, as in Jude 12. The early church shared fellowship meals, often with the Lord’s Supper, and the false teachers took part, turning sacred fellowship into self-indulgence.

Eyes full of adultery. Literally eyes full of an adulteress: men who cannot look at a woman without sizing her up as a possible conquest (Matthew 5:28). And insatiable, akatapaustous, never resting. That is the cruelty of every lust: it promises rest and delivers restlessness.

They entice unsteady souls. Entice, deleazontes, is the fishing and hunting word: to bait, as in James 1:14. Unsteady, astēriktous, is the opposite of the established believers of 1:12. New or weak believers are their targets: predators select carefully.

Hearts trained in greed. Trained, gegymnasmenēn, is the athlete’s word, the root of gymnasium. This is not a lapse but a discipline, worked at until it comes naturally. The same word is used in Hebrews 5:14 of mature believers whose powers of discernment are trained by constant practice. Everyone is in training for something.

Accursed children! Literally children of a curse: a Hebrew way of saying people under God’s curse. Peter’s exclamation is not a loss of temper but a cry of horror at what these men have become, and at where they are taking others.

Why is the Bible’s language about these men so harsh? Because the stakes are so high. These men are leading souls to destruction while feasting at the Lord’s Table. A shepherd who finds wolves among the flock does not describe them gently (Acts 20:29). Jesus spoke the same way of the scribes and Pharisees who shut the kingdom in people’s faces (Matthew 23). The harshness is love for the sheep. But note that it is aimed at those who teach and exploit, not at ordinary strugglers; to the weak and the wandering Scripture speaks with great tenderness (Matthew 12:20).

I struggle with lustful eyes. Am I like these men? There is a world of difference between a believer who fights lust and hates it, and a man whose eyes are full of it, who is insatiable, trains himself in it and teaches others to indulge. The first is a wounded soldier; the second is a deserter who has gone over to the enemy. A believer can both love a sin and hate it at once, and that inner war is itself the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:15–25; Galatians 5:17). If you are fighting, keep fighting: make a covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1), cut off what feeds it, bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and run to Christ each time you fall. The very fact that you grieve shows that you are not what this verse describes.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are training yourself in by your habits: what you watch, what you scroll, what you spend on, what you daydream about. Not by willpower alone: the Spirit who made you a partaker of the divine nature trains you through the word, prayer and the company of believers, so replace one habit of the flesh with one habit of grace. You will not do it perfectly. Christ’s clean eyes and pure heart were his perfect obedience in your place, and they are counted as yours; so when you fail, begin again.

For worship. Every line of this portrait has its opposite in him. His eyes were full of compassion and never of lust; his food was to do his Father’s will, and it satisfied him; he did not bait the unsteady but gathered them, and carried the lambs in his arms. Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor. And children of a curse are exactly the people he came for. He bore the curse himself, so that the accursed might be called children of God and sit at his table, washed, filled and welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forsaking the right way. The right way is the straight road. Gone astray, eplanēthēsan, gives us planet, a wandering star. They knew the road, and they left it.

The way of Balaam. Most manuscripts, followed by the KJV, call his father Bosor, a variant form of the name; a few early ones read Beor, as in Numbers. Balaam is the exact case: a soothsayer to whom God really spoke (Joshua 13:22; Numbers 22:9–12), and who put that gift on the market. The story is in Numbers 22–24. Balak of Moab offers money to have Israel cursed; Balaam keeps asking God for permission to go; the narrative hints that he wants the fee, and the New Testament says so outright. In the end he cannot curse; every time he opens his mouth, blessing comes out. But he later advises Balak how to lead Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry at Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; 31:16; Revelation 2:14), which is what he is remembered for (Jude 11).

Who loved gain from wrongdoing. Literally loved the wages of unrighteousness, echoing verse 13. It identifies the false teachers precisely: not men who set out to destroy the church but men who discovered that religion pays and adjusted their message to keep it paying. And the verb is loved. The problem was not that he was paid, but what he loved.

A speechless donkey. A voiceless beast of burden producing a human voice, and the reversal is the point. The irrational animal of verse 12 had more sense than the prophet. The prophet is behaving like an animal, so an animal has to do the prophet’s job (Numbers 22:21–35). Madness, paraphronia, is being out of one’s mind. Balaam was not deceived; he had heard from God repeatedly and went anyway. The man who knows exactly what God has said and calculates that the money is worth it has lost his reason, whatever his gifts.

A star out of Jacob. The most remarkable thing Balaam ever said, he said against his will. Hired to curse, he was made to see far ahead: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17). The man who loved wages was made to announce the King whose sceptre no money could buy. God can put the truth about his Son even into a mercenary’s mouth, but Balaam saw the star from far off and died among the enemies of the people it would rise over (Numbers 31:8). To see Christ and not love him is the deepest madness of all.

The mercy in the road. There is a mercy in the story too, easily missed. The angel stood in the road with a drawn sword, and the donkey turned aside three times and saved his life (Numbers 22:33). Even a man this far gone was given an obstacle in the road. God often puts such obstacles in our way: a closed door, a rebuke, an illness, a word from an unexpected mouth. The question is whether we beat the donkey or listen to it.

How do I know whether I love money too much? Ask a few honest questions. Would I compromise truth or conscience to keep or gain it? Do I give generously and gladly, or grudgingly? Does the thought of losing it fill me with fear? Does it shape my decisions more than God’s word does? Do I resent others who have more? Love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10), and it hides well, especially in religious people. The cure is not only to hold it loosely but to love something better: to find Christ so satisfying that money returns to its proper place as a tool and not a god.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all who are paid for ministry are like Balaam. Workers deserve wages (1 Timothy 5:18). The sin is loving money and compromising truth for it.

On a Tuesday. A bank statement can be read as a spiritual document: what does yours say you love?
verseByVerse.note: Balaam was hired to curse Israel for money, and his donkey spoke to rebuke him.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Waterless springs. Two images, and both are about promise without delivery. In that country a spring was life. To walk to one in the heat and find it dry is not disappointment but danger. God had complained through Jeremiah that his people had forsaken him, the fountain of living waters, and dug broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). False teachers are such cisterns.

Mists driven by a storm. The same failure in the sky. Clouds driven by a squall raise every farmer’s hope and pass over without rain, and Jude uses the same picture (Jude 12). These men are weather that does not break.

The gloom of utter darkness. The destiny of the false teachers is outer darkness (Matthew 8:12; 22:13; Jude 13). Reserved, tetērētai, is the custody word from verses 4 and 9: set aside and waiting. And there is a grim fitness: men who promised light are held in the dark.

Loud boasts of folly. Loud boasts, hyperonka, are swelling, bombastic words; folly, mataiotēs, is emptiness, the word Paul uses of creation subjected to futility (Romans 8:20). Impressive-sounding but empty, like a drum, and delivered confidently, which is what makes it work on people who are unsure. And the bait is not intellectual; it is appetite.

Barely escaping. Oligōs apopheugontas is only a little escaping: new converts who have just left paganism. (The KJV’s clean escaped follows later manuscripts with a word meaning truly.) That is the cruelty of it. New converts, still unsteady, having just broken with a way of life at real cost, are told they need not have bothered.

They promise them freedom. Probably a twisted version of Christian freedom, claiming that grace means freedom from moral rules (Galatians 5:13; 1 Peter 2:16; Romans 6:1–2). It is the oldest lie in the world, the serpent’s promise in the garden: throw off God’s word and your eyes will be opened.

Slaves of corruption. Corruption, phthora, is the moral decay of 1:4, which believers escaped. The irony is sharp: Peter called himself a slave of Christ in 1:1, and these men, who promise freedom, are slaves of rot.

Whatever overcomes a person. Overcomes, hēttētai, is a word from the battlefield: the conquered become the slaves of the conqueror. A proverb, and a searching one: whatever masters you is your master (Romans 6:16). Freedom is not the absence of a master; it is a question of which one. The man who has thrown off restraint has not become free. He has changed owners, and taken a worse one. Jesus said it first, and gave the only way out: everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin, and if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). The serpent offered freedom by throwing off God’s word; the Son gives it by breaking the old master’s hold at the cost of his own life, and taking his freed people under a yoke that is easy (Matthew 11:29–30).

What does real Christian freedom look like? It is freedom from the guilt of sin, because Christ has paid for it; freedom from the power of sin, because we are united to him; freedom from the law as a way of earning acceptance; and freedom from fear of death and judgement. But it is freedom for something: to love God and serve others (Galatians 5:13). A train is free on its rails and helpless off them; a fish is free in water and dies on the bank. We are free when we live as we were made to live, under the gentle rule of Christ, whose yoke is easy.

I have just come to faith and feel shaky. How do I avoid being lured? Stay close to the flock and to faithful shepherds; predators pick off the sheep that wander alone. Get into a Bible-teaching church and attend faithfully. Read Scripture daily, starting with a Gospel. Find an older believer to meet with and ask questions. Be wary of anyone who tells you that the sins you have left were not really so bad, or that grace means you need not change. And when temptation comes dressed as freedom, ask where it leads; the end of the road is what tells you the truth about it.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you reach for without thinking when you are bored, anxious or lonely; that is often the master. Then tell Christ plainly that you want him to rule there, and take one practical step to break its grip.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After they have escaped. These verses are among the most sobering in the New Testament. They are the false teachers, and perhaps those they led astray. Escaped is the word of 1:4; defilements, miasmata, are pollutions. Whatever these men were, they were not outsiders. They had genuinely got out of their former life, at the level anyone could see, and they had known the gospel through the letter’s key word, knowledge, understood it, perhaps professed it.

Again entangled and overcome. Entangled, emplakentes, is woven in, like a fish in a net or a man in thorns. Overcome is the word of verse 19: conquered again by the master they once escaped.

The last state worse than the first. Peter is echoing his Master’s words about a house swept clean and reoccupied by seven worse spirits, so that the last state is worse than the first (Matthew 12:45; Luke 11:26). Having known the truth and rejected it, they are more guilty and more hardened than before.

Better never to have known. That is the plain sense, and it should not be blunted. Greater knowledge brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:47–48; Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29): a man who has seen and turned away is in a worse position than one who never saw. The holy commandment is the Christian faith and way of life, delivered by the apostles (Jude 3). It was handed to them, like a precious thing passed from hand to hand, and they put it down.

The true proverb. How does this stand with the perseverance of the saints, the teaching that those God truly saves he keeps to the end? Peter himself supplies the answer, and it is the reason the proverb is there.

The dog returns to its own vomit. From Proverbs 26:11. In Jewish eyes dogs were mostly scavengers, despised as unclean. The dog gets rid of what was making it sick, and then goes back to it, because it is still a dog.

The sow, after washing herself. A popular proverb. Look at what has and has not changed. The sow has been washed: genuinely, outwardly, and everyone could see it. What she has not been given is a different nature. She returns to the mud because she is still a pig, and washing a pig does not make it a sheep. The false teachers were outwardly cleaned, but their nature was never changed. That is Peter’s verdict on such men: not that they lost salvation, but that they were cleaned rather than changed. The escape was real at the level of behaviour, and the heart was never renewed, which is exactly what 1 John 2:19 says of those who went out from us because they were not of us.

Clean, but not every one of you. Peter had heard this distinction drawn by the Lord himself, the night his own feet were washed. The one who has bathed, Jesus said, is completely clean; and you are clean, but not every one of you, for he knew who was to betray him (John 13:10–11). Judas, it seems, had his feet washed by the hands of Christ, and went out into the night. Outward washing, even at Jesus’ hands, is not belonging to him. The cleansing that changes a nature is the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ our Saviour (Titus 3:5–6).

In the flow. The chapter ends by turning the language of chapter 1 inside out. There believers had escaped the corruption that is in the world (1:4); here men have escaped its defilements and been dragged back. There the knowledge of Christ made lives fruitful (1:8); here the same knowledge, held without a changed heart, only adds to guilt. And the warning prepares chapter 3, where Peter tells his beloved readers to take care that they are not carried away and lose their own stability (3:17). His remedy is not anxiety but the growth he urged in 1:5–11 and urges again in his last sentence (3:18).

Where Christians differ: does this passage show that true believers can lose salvation? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer may finally turn away and be lost, read the passage so, pointing to escaped and to knowledge of our Lord and Saviour. Many of them are earnest, godly believers, and the warning they stress is real. Verdict: The proverbs answer the question. The dog and the sow returned to filth because their nature had never been changed; they were washed outwardly but remained dogs and pigs. These people had external knowledge of Christ and outward moral reform, but never received a new nature (1:4). True believers, made partakers of the divine nature, are kept by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5) and will never finally fall (1:10). Those who return permanently to their former life show they were never truly regenerated (1 John 2:19).

How can someone know so much and never be truly saved? Because knowing about Christ is not the same as being united to him. Judas walked with Jesus for about three years, heard every sermon and saw every miracle. People can be moved by the gospel, reform their habits, join a church, even teach, and yet never have been born again (Matthew 7:21–23; 13:20–21). The difference is not how much they knew but whether the Spirit gave them a new heart. That is why the test is not how impressive a conversion looked, but what a person keeps returning to over time.

I have gone back to an old sin. Am I the dog returning to its vomit? Not if you hate it and want to be free. The dog returns to its vomit gladly, because it is what a dog loves. A child of God may fall back into sin, sometimes badly and repeatedly, but he is miserable there, he confesses it, and he longs to be clean (Psalm 51; 1 John 1:9). Peter himself denied Christ three times and was restored. If you are grieved, go to Christ today. He has not changed his mind about you, and the new nature in you is the very thing that makes the mud unbearable.

On a Tuesday. This passage is meant not to make secure believers anxious but to make everyone honest. Its question is not whether you have been washed but whether you have been changed, and the evidence is what you find yourself returning to when you are tired, alone and unwatched. Thank God for every sign that you now love what you once hated; and where the old pull remains, bring it to him today.

For worship. He did not merely wash us; he made us new. The Lord Jesus does not wash pigs and leave them pigs. He gives a new heart and puts a new spirit within, so that what we once loved becomes our grief, and what we once despised becomes our joy. The dog returns to its vomit; the sheep returns to its Shepherd, because his voice is the one it now loves, and no one will snatch it out of his hand.

2.theology: The chapter’s controlling question is apostasy: can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer is that those truly born again will persevere (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:38–39). But the visible church contains people who share its privileges without its life, and it is these who can have the knowledge described in verse 20 and still return to their former state. The dog and the sow mark the boundary: the animal’s nature is unchanged. Outward reform without a new heart ends in worse corruption. This is not a loophole in the doctrine of perseverance; it is the setting in which the doctrine is honestly held.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives a congregation a plain test. What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Is the teaching shaped by what people want to hear, and will pay to hear? Balaam’s gift was real, but it became a commodity. The test of a ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
The last chapter is the letter’s goal. The false teachers are dangerous because they attack the hope of Christ’s return, and with it the reason for holy living. If no day is coming, why be holy?

Peter answers in three steps. The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word created it and judged it by the flood, and the same word holds it now for judgment. God is not slow, but patient, giving time for repentance. And the day will come suddenly and lay everything bare. So the question is not “When?” but “What sort of people ought you to be?” The letter ends: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever.
3.text: <sup>1</sup>This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder,<sup>2</sup>that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,<sup>3</sup>knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires.<sup>4</sup>They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."<sup>5</sup>For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God,<sup>6</sup>and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.<sup>7</sup>But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.<sup>8</sup>But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.<sup>9</sup>The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.<sup>10</sup>But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.<sup>11</sup>Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness,<sup>12</sup>waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn!<sup>13</sup>But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.<sup>15</sup>And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him,<sup>16</sup>as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.<sup>17</sup>You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability.<sup>18</sup>But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Scoffers and the Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter reminds his readers of the prophets and the apostles, and warns that scoffers will mock the promise of Christ’s coming. He answers them from creation and the flood, from God’s relation to time, and from his patience, and warns that the day will still come like a thief.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Slowness but Patience

The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word made it and judged it by the flood. The Lord is not slow but patient, and the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scoffers pointed to the death of the first generation as proof that nothing was coming.

Now: The delay is mercy; the right response is repentance, not argument about the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Peter 3 answers the denial of Christ’s return and calls believers to holy living as they wait. Peter reminds them of the prophets and the apostles (vv. 1–2). Scoffers will mock the promise of his coming, saying nothing has changed since creation (vv. 3–4); but God made the world by his word and judged it once by water, and by the same word the present heavens and earth are kept for fire (vv. 5–7). With the Lord a day is as a thousand years; his delay is patience, not wishing any to perish (vv. 8–9). The day of the Lord will come like a thief, and the earth and its works will be exposed (v. 10). So live holy lives, waiting for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells (vv. 11–13), be found spotless and at peace, counting his patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote (vv. 14–16). Do not be carried away, but grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever (vv. 17–18).

The second letter. The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter, and Peter treats both as one project with one aim. Beloved, agapētoi, comes four times in this chapter (vv. 1, 8, 14, 17), a warm contrast with the harsh words about false teachers. Having described the wolves, the shepherd turns to the sheep and his voice changes.

Stirring up your sincere mind. Stirring up, diegeirō, is the waking verb again from 1:13: his readers do not need new material; they need rousing. Sincere, eilikrinē, means pure, unmixed. It is often explained as judged by sunlight, as pottery was held up to the sun to check for cracks, though that origin is uncertain. Unlike the false teachers, the readers have pure minds, and Peter credits them with genuineness even as he warns them. A sound mind is not a mind beyond the reach of drowsiness.

The predictions of the holy prophets. The Old Testament prophets foretold the Day of the Lord, judgement and new creation (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; Joel 2; Daniel 7; 12). And the whole defence against what follows is memory: not a new argument but the recollection of what they were already told.

Through your apostles. The commandment is the apostolic teaching, including Christ’s promise to return, and they are your apostles: not a distant institution but the men who actually brought them the gospel. Here are two authorities, set side by side without any suggestion that they differ in weight: the Old Testament prophets, and the apostles carrying the Lord’s own commandment. That is a significant sentence for how the early church understood its own writings, and Peter will do it explicitly with Paul’s letters in verse 16. The two together form the foundation (Ephesians 2:20). And they meet in one Person. The risen Lord opened his disciples’ minds to see that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44–45); the prophets foretold him, the apostles were sent by him, and the commandment is his own.

Why does it matter that the prophets and apostles are put together? Because it means the whole Bible speaks with one voice and one authority. The Old Testament is not a lesser, outdated book, and the New Testament is not merely the church’s opinion about Jesus. Both are God’s word. So when you read about the day of the Lord in Joel or Zephaniah and then in Peter, you are hearing one story told by one Author, promised in the one and explained in the other. Read them together, and let each shed light on the other.

On a Tuesday. Pick one promise of Christ’s return and read it each morning this week: Acts 1:11, John 14:3, or Isaiah 65:17–25. Let it wake you. And thank God for whoever first brought you the apostles’ message; that person was your Peter.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing this first of all. As in 1:20. Before you hear the scoffers, know that they were foretold.

Scoffers will come in the last days. Scoffers with scoffing, empaiktai en empaigmonē: mockers mocking, a Hebrew-style emphasis. And their arrival is itself predicted. Every scoffer is, without meaning to be, a fulfilled prophecy. The last days are the whole period since Christ’s first coming (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; Jude 18). The scoffers were already present in Peter’s day, and they are with us still.

Following their own sinful desires. Peter names the motive before he states the argument, and the order is deliberate. Their doctrine has a cause, and the cause is not intellectual: if there is no coming judgement, there is no reason to restrain oneself. A man who wants the future to be empty has a reason for wanting it. Peter is describing these particular mockers; he is not saying that every honest doubter is hiding a sin.

They will say, Where is the promise of his coming? Then the taunt itself. “Promise of his coming” (hē epangelia tēs parousias autou) is Jesus’ promise to return (John 14:3; Acts 1:11). The mocking question echoes Old Testament scoffers, who asked the psalmist all the day long where his God was (Psalm 42:3), and who asked, where is the God of justice? (Malachi 2:17).

The promise was his own. The scoffers are mocking not a church doctrine but the word of Jesus: I will come again and will take you to myself (John 14:3). They are not the first to mock his promises. At the cross the chief priests jeered, he saved others; he cannot save himself (Matthew 27:42), and afterwards called him the impostor who had said he would rise after three days (Matthew 27:63). On the third day the tomb was empty. The promise mocked once was kept once, and that is the pledge of the next: God has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31).

Ever since the fathers fell asleep. The fathers are probably the first generation of Christians, who had died, or perhaps the Old Testament patriarchs. Fell asleep, ekoimēthēsan, a common Christian word for dying (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15), already carries the hope of waking. Sleep describes the body, and how temporary death is; it does not mean the soul lies unconscious, for to depart is to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). The argument has two parts and both would have stung. The first is that the first generation had died and nothing had happened. It was a real pastoral problem in a church burying its founders. Many scholars take this line as a sign that the letter was written after the apostles’ generation had died, and so after Peter. But by the mid-60s many first believers had died, Stephen and James among them, and if the fathers are the patriarchs the phrase says nothing about date at all.

All things are continuing as they were. The second part is a philosophy: things go on as they always have. It is the argument from uniformity: the world is a closed system running on unbroken regularity; God does not intervene; what has never been observed to happen therefore does not happen; there will be no judgement. That is a very modern-sounding argument to find in a first-century letter. Peter’s answer does not dispute the observation that the sun rises every morning. He disputes the conclusion, by pointing to two occasions when things did not continue as they were.

Is it wrong to wonder why Christ has not yet come? No. Honest questions are not scoffing. The souls under the altar cry, how long? (Revelation 6:10), and the psalms are full of it. What Peter condemns is mocking unbelief that uses the delay as an excuse to live as one pleases. The difference lies in the heart: the scoffer asks where is he? hoping the answer is nowhere; the believer asks where is he? because he longs to see him. If your question comes from longing, it is a kind of prayer: come, Lord Jesus.

How should I answer someone who says the world just runs by natural laws? Agree that the world is wonderfully regular, and then ask why. The regularity of nature is not an argument against God but evidence of his faithful upholding of all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3; Genesis 8:22). Laws describe how things normally go; they do not forbid the Lawgiver from acting. And history itself is not a closed loop: it had a beginning, it has seen a resurrection, and Scripture says it is moving toward an end. Be gentle, and point the conversation to Jesus’ resurrection, which is the decisive interruption.

On a Tuesday. Is there any area of your life where you live as though he were not coming, because you would rather he did not see it yet? Bring that into the light today; he who is coming forgives all who confess (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They deliberately overlook this fact. Lanthanei thelontas: this escapes their notice because they want it to. Their ignorance is chosen (Romans 1:18–21). Peter does not accuse them of missing the evidence but of declining to look at it, which is the more serious charge.

By the word of God. The first fact they ignore: God made the world by his word (Genesis 1; Hebrews 11:3), and in Genesis 1 the earth emerged from the waters (1:2, 6–10). The world is not self-existent or eternal; it depends on God’s word. The claim that all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation collapses at the word creation. There was a beginning, and it was not a continuation of anything.

Deluged with water and perished. The second fact they ignore: the flood. Deluged, kataklystheis, gives us cataclysm. The same water that the world was formed through later destroyed it, which is exactly a case of things not continuing as they were. So the argument is complete in two strokes. The scoffers say nothing has ever interrupted the regularity; Peter names two occasions when the world’s entire state was changed by the word of God, and both are in the Scriptures the scoffers claim to respect.

Was the flood worldwide? Genesis describes a flood that covered all the high mountains under the whole heaven (Genesis 7:19), and Peter sets it beside the coming judgement of the whole earth by fire (2 Peter 3:6–7). Most Christians have read it as worldwide, while some godly scholars hold that it covered the whole inhabited region rather than the whole earth. On either reading it was a real judgement, and Noah’s rescue a real salvation.

By the same word. Everything in the passage hangs on the phrase. One agency made it, one flooded it, and one holds it now. The present stability is not inertia; it is sustained by the same voice that could end it. Stored up, tethēsaurismenoi, is treasured up, as in a treasury. And the next judgement will be by fire, not water: God promised Noah never again to destroy the earth by a flood (Genesis 9:11), and the prophets speak of fire (Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

The Word who holds it. The New Testament puts a face on the same word. All things were made through the eternal Word (John 1:3), and the Son upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3). So the word that formed the earth out of water, and now holds it for fire, is the voice of the Son. The world is kept for judgement by the Lord who will be revealed from heaven in flaming fire (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). And for the same reason the waiting world is kept for mercy: the one who holds back the fire is the Son who came the first time not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17).

Being kept until the day of judgment. Kept, tēroumenoi, is the custody word again, as of the angels in 2:4. Peter’s picture of the present universe is not a machine running down but something held in reserve. Destruction, apōleia, is ruin: for the ungodly, eternal ruin.

What it does not mean. Destruction does not mean annihilation of the ungodly. Scripture describes their punishment as eternal and conscious (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11; 20:10). The word means ruin, loss of all that makes existence good. Some evangelical Christians hold that the lost will finally cease to exist; this commentary respects them but holds the historic view, chiefly because Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46).

Should a Christian fear that the world will end in a nuclear war or climate disaster? We should care for God’s creation and work for peace, because we are stewards of what he made. But we need not live in terror that human beings will end the world before God’s time. The heavens and earth are kept by his word for his day. History will not end by accident or by our hand, but when and as he has appointed. That frees us both from despair and from the burden of thinking we must save the planet ourselves. Do your duty calmly, and trust the Keeper.

For worship. He spoke, and the waters parted and the dry land appeared. He spoke again, and the fountains of the deep broke open. He speaks still, and the stars keep their courses and the earth its seasons, held in reserve by the word that made them. And for his people the coming fire holds no terror, because judgement has already broken over another: the Son bore in his own body the wrath that their sins had stored up. Blessed be the God who made the world by a word, and will make it new by the same.

verseByVerse.quote: But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not overlook this one fact. The same verb he used of the scoffers in verse 5, now turned round with an endearment attached. The scoffers deliberately forget; believers must not.

One day is as a thousand years. The line echoes Psalm 90:4: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past. God is eternal, not bound by time as we are. We must not judge his faithfulness by our timetable. To a creature with seventy or eighty years, a delay of two millennia seems decisive; to the One who made time it is not a delay at all. The scoffers’ argument depends entirely on assuming God experiences duration the way they do.

Both halves are needed. The comparison runs both ways, which would make any arithmetic useless. A thousand years as one day means the long wait is nothing to him. One day as a thousand years means no single day is trivial to him either: he is not distracted or inattentive during the interval. He gives each day of your life the attention of a thousand years.

The Lord of the thousand years. Peter’s Lord is not a distant clock-keeper. The one for whom a thousand years are as a day is the Son who could say, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), and who then lived some thirty years of ordinary days in Nazareth before his hour came. Eternity did not merely watch time; it entered it, so the delay of his coming is not the absence of someone who cannot feel the wait. And if any single day has carried the weight of a thousand years, it was the day he said, it is finished (John 19:30).

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach a thousand-year day or a millennial scheme? Some have used this verse to calculate the timing of Christ’s return, such as six thousand years of history followed by a thousand-year millennium. Verdict: The verse is not a formula for calculation; it teaches that God’s perspective on time differs from ours. It warns against date-setting, not encourages it (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7). It gives no support to elaborate millennial timetables. (Christians differ on the thousand years of Revelation 20 itself, whether it is a future earthly reign of Christ or his present reign from heaven; this verse does not decide that question.)

Does this mean that the days of creation were long ages? This verse does not say so. Peter is speaking of how God relates to time, to explain the delay of Christ’s coming; the verse is not a conversion table, and reading it as one has produced a great deal of confusion. The days of Genesis 1 must be read from Genesis itself, and read there they are six ordinary days: each is numbered and closed with evening and morning, and the fourth commandment grounds our working week in God’s six days of making (Exodus 20:11). Whatever view a Christian takes of that question, this verse does not settle it, because it is not about creation at all. This commentary holds that God made all things in six ordinary days. Other faithful Christians read the days as long ages, as a literary framework for the week of creation, or as God’s workdays described by analogy with ours, often because they weigh the evidence for an old earth or the careful shape of the chapter; they deserve a patient hearing, and all agree that God made all things by his word.

Why would God make his people wait so long? Peter gives the main answer in the next verse: patience, so that more may repent. But consider too that waiting is how God grows faith. Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac; Israel waited centuries for the Messiah; Simeon waited, perhaps for many years, to hold the child. In the waiting, God tests and refines his people, teaches them to walk by faith and not sight, and gathers in his elect. The wait is long to us, but it is not empty. It is full of his purposes.

On a Tuesday. Think of a prayer you have prayed for years without an answer. Pray it again today, not with resignation but with confidence that he has not forgotten one day of it.
