verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not slow to fulfill his promise. Slow, bradynei, is to delay, loiter. Peter denies the premise directly, with a qualifier: as some count. The slowness exists only in the reckoning of the people complaining.

But is patient toward you. Here is the positive answer, the heart of the chapter. Patient, makrothymei, is literally long of temper, slow to anger. Toward you: the readers, God’s beloved people (v. 1), the chosen (1 Peter 1:1). The delay is not indifference, not incapacity, and not forgetfulness. It is patience, and it is directed at them. Every day the end has not come is a day granted. The scoffers were treating the interval as evidence against God; Peter says it is evidence of his mercy, and that they are standing inside the very thing they are mocking.

Not wishing that any should perish. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11), and his patience gives time for repentance, metanoia, a change of mind and direction (Romans 2:4).

The patience of our Lord. Peter will tell them to count the patience of our Lord as salvation (v. 15), and the New Testament shows that patience with a human face. Paul, once a persecutor, wrote that he received mercy so that in him, the foremost of sinners, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15–16). The long temper of God is not the Father holding back an impatient Son. It is the patience of the Saviour himself, who wept over Jerusalem, prayed for those who crucified him, and reigns now while the last of his sheep are gathered in.

In the flow. Verses 8 and 9 give two answers to the scoffers’ question in verse 4. Verse 8 answers from God’s relation to time: the wait is not long to him. Verse 9 answers from his heart: the wait is mercy. Then verse 10 adds the warning that keeps the mercy from being misread, for the day will still come like a thief, and verse 15 turns the same truth into a command: count the patience of our Lord as salvation.

Where Christians differ: if God wishes all to repent, why are not all saved? Arminians read this verse as showing that God wills every individual to be saved and that human choice makes the difference; universalists as showing that all will eventually be saved. Reformed and Arminian Christians have long differed here, and both want to honour God’s mercy. Verdict: The context helps: God is patient toward you, addressing believers, the beloved, the elect. The delay of Christ’s return is so that all of God’s people, including those not yet converted, may come to repentance before the end. When the last of the elect has been brought in, Christ will return. At the same time, Scripture teaches that God sincerely desires the repentance of all sinners in the sense that he delights in repentance and offers the gospel freely to all (Ezekiel 33:11; 1 Timothy 2:4), while he has also sovereignly chosen to save some and not all. These two truths, God’s revealed desire and his decreed purpose, are both taught, and must both be held. Universalism contradicts the next verse and the clear teaching of eternal judgement.

The use of the verse. On either emphasis the pastoral use is the same. What neither permits is the conclusion the scoffers wanted, that the delay means nothing is coming. If God is holding the door open, the response of anyone still outside it is not to argue about the mechanism but to walk through.

If God has chosen his elect, why should I evangelise? Because God has chosen the means as well as the end. The elect are brought to repentance through the gospel being preached (Romans 10:14–17), and God waits so that the gospel may reach them. Election is the great encouragement to evangelism, not its enemy: Paul was told to keep speaking in Corinth because the Lord had many people in that city (Acts 18:9–10). You do not know who the elect are, so offer Christ freely to everyone, sincerely, as God himself does. Every day of patience is a day for the gospel.

I have a loved one who has not repented. Is it too late? Not while they are alive, and not while the Lord is patient. This verse is a reason to keep praying and keep loving. God waited for you, perhaps for years. He knows how to bring the hardest heart to repentance, as he did with Saul of Tarsus. So pray specifically, live kindly before them, speak of Christ when doors open, and leave the timing with God. His patience is not reluctance to save; it is room being made for repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a thief. The day of the Lord is the Old Testament term for God’s great day of judgement and salvation (Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18–20; Zephaniah 1:14–18), now identified with Christ’s return. The thief image is the Lord’s own (Matthew 24:43), and Paul and John use it too (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 16:15). What it conveys is not stealth for its own sake but unpredictability: the one thing about a burglary that you cannot prepare for is the timing. This thief does not come quietly; the next clause says the heavens will roar. And it answers the scoffers’ question exactly. They asked where the promise was; Peter says the promise includes the fact that you will not see it coming.

With a roar. Pass away, pareleusontai, is the word Jesus used: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matthew 24:35). With a roar, rhoizēdon, imitates its sound: a rushing noise, like an arrow in flight, the whirring of wings, the crackle of a great fire.

Burned up and dissolved. The heavenly bodies, stoicheia, elements, are either the basic elements of the physical world, or the sun, moon and stars (Isaiah 34:4). Dissolved, lythēsetai, is the word for untying something. Either way the dissolution of the present order is total.

Will be exposed. The last clause is the most important in the verse. Exposed, heurethēsetai, is will be found, laid bare. It changes the picture from mere destruction to disclosure. The fire is not chiefly an incinerator but a searchlight. Everything done on this earth will be brought into the open before God’s judgement (1 Corinthians 3:13; Hebrews 4:13), and the eyes that see it will be his: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), the one whose eyes are like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14). A universe that simply burns cancels the record; a universe that is laid bare produces it. Peter’s point against men who were living as they pleased is not only that the world will end but that it will be examined. That is hard news for a heart that lives for its reputation, because what other people think of us is exactly what the fire will not consult. And it is good news for anyone who has been wronged in secret and never vindicated: on that day the truth will come out.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ at the end of this verse. The oldest read will be found or exposed (heurethēsetai); later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read will be burned up (katakaēsetai); some read will not be found. The more difficult reading, will be found, is most likely original, meaning laid bare before God’s judgement.

Where Christians differ: is the day of the Lord a single event? Dispensationalists (who see God’s plan in distinct stages, with separate futures for Israel and the church) often separate a secret rapture of the church from a later visible return, and place a thousand-year earthly kingdom between Christ’s return and the final judgement and new creation. Other premillennial Christians, who reject a secret rapture, still see a sequence: Christ’s return, a thousand-year reign, then the final judgement and new creation. Verdict: Peter places Christ’s coming, the day of the Lord, the judgement of the ungodly, and the dissolution of the present heavens and earth together in one great event, followed by the new heavens and new earth (vv. 7, 10, 12–13). This fits the amillennial understanding (that the thousand years of Revelation 20 describe Christ’s present reign, not a later earthly kingdom): one visible return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, all are judged, and creation is renewed. There is no secret rapture and no intervening earthly millennium. Many faithful Christians hold premillennial or dispensational views, and every one of them shares the hope this chapter teaches: Christ is coming, visibly and in glory, and his people must be ready. This commentary differs from them on the order of events, not on the hope.

If he comes like a thief, does that not mean a secret coming? No. The thief image describes the timing, not the manner. The same Lord who said he would come like a thief said that his coming would be like lightning flashing from east to west (Matthew 24:27), and that every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). Here in Peter, the thief’s arrival is accompanied by the roar of the heavens. It will be sudden for everyone and secret to no one. That is why believers need not fear being left behind in a silent disappearance; we are called instead to be ready at any hour for a return that will fill the sky.

Will the earth then be annihilated, or renewed? Some Christians hold that the old creation will be destroyed and replaced, pointing to pass away and dissolved. But Peter compares it to the flood, which cleansed the world rather than abolishing it (v. 6), and says the earth will be exposed, laid bare to judgement. Paul says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:21). The more likely reading is that the present creation will be purged by fire and renewed, not abolished.

Should I try to work out when it will happen? No. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and that it is not for us to know the times or seasons the Father has fixed (Acts 1:7). Every attempt to set dates has failed and brought the faith into ridicule. The signs Jesus gave (wars, false teachers, persecution, the gospel to the nations) mark the whole age, so that every generation should be ready. Scripture also names some things that come first: the gospel preached to all nations (Matthew 24:14), and a great falling away with the man of lawlessness revealed (2 Thessalonians 2:1–4). So his coming is near and always to be expected, yet not without named events before it, and never to be dated. The right response to a thief who comes at an unknown hour is not to calculate the hour but to keep the house ready at all hours.

On a Tuesday. If Christ came today, what would be exposed in your life? For a believer that is not a reason for terror, because Christ has already borne what the fire would find; but it is a reason to deal with the thing you would hurry to hide: confess it, put it right, or remove it. Then you will be able to say, with an easier heart, come, Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — New Heavens, and the Last Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since everything will be dissolved and laid bare, Peter asks what kind of people believers should be: holy and godly, waiting for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home. They are to be found at peace, count the Lord’s patience as salvation, read Paul humbly rather than twist him, and, forewarned, grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ, to whom be glory for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Answer to Error Is Growth

Since everything will be laid bare, live in holiness and godliness while waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. The last command is to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter called Paul a beloved brother and counted his letters among the Scriptures.

Now: A growing believer is far harder to uproot than one who is merely on guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these things are thus to be dissolved. A present participle: being loosed, as good as dissolving already. Everything you can see has a date stamped on it that you cannot read.

What sort of people ought you to be. Peter draws the practical conclusion, and what he does not draw is telling. Not speculation, not date-setting, not withdrawal. The question is about character. Holiness, hagiais anastrophais, is holy ways of life, and it is plural: in every area. Holiness is not a churchy manner or a mood. It means belonging to God and becoming like him: as he who called you is holy, Peter had written, be holy in all your conduct (1 Peter 1:15). Godliness is plural too: acts of godliness, the concrete and repeated, not a general disposition. Eschatology, the teaching about the last things, is not for speculation but for transformation (1 John 3:2–3). If the house is to be pulled down, you do not spend your life polishing its brass; you invest in what will last.

Waiting for and hastening. Waiting, prosdokōntas, is looking for eagerly, as a family watches the road for a returning son. Hastening, speudontas, is startling. It can mean to be eager for, but its ordinary sense is to hurry, to speed something up. And Peter has just said the delay is God’s patience, waiting for people to reach repentance. Believers can, in some sense, hasten the day: by holy living, by prayer (your kingdom come, Matthew 6:10), and by evangelism, which brings in the elect whose conversion the Lord awaits (v. 9; Matthew 24:14). God has ordained the means as well as the end. That is a dignity given to ordinary Christian obedience.

Will melt as they burn! The description is repeated, and it is bleak, until verse 13 turns it round. Melt, tēketai, as in Isaiah 34:4 in the Greek, and Micah 1:4, where the mountains melt under the LORD like wax before the fire.

New heavens and a new earth. There is the point of the whole passage, and it is his promise (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). The scoffers asked, where is the promise? Peter answers: here it is. New, kainous, suggests new in quality, renewed: not merely a new universe in time, but a transformed one in kind (Revelation 21:1–5; Romans 8:19–21). The fire is not the end of the story, and it is not the destruction of the material world as such. What follows is a new earth: physical, real, and renewed, exactly as Isaiah promised, with resurrected people in resurrected bodies living in a world set free.

In which righteousness dwells. Dwells, katoikei, is settles down, makes its permanent home. In the present world righteousness is a visitor often turned away at the door; in the new creation it will be at home. No more sin, injustice, evil or death (Revelation 21:4, 27). And that single clause is the answer to everything chapter 2 described. Peter has spent a chapter on men who exploited the church and seemed to get away with it. The world that is coming is one where righteousness is resident. And righteousness at home means the Righteous One at home among his people: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3).

What will the new heavens and new earth actually be like? Scripture gives us glimpses rather than a map, but the glimpses are glorious. It will be a real, physical world, this creation renewed, as our risen bodies will be these bodies glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). God will dwell with his people; there will be no more tears, death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:3–4). There will be work without frustration, worship without weariness, fellowship without sin, and the glory of the nations brought in (Revelation 21:24–26). Above all, we will see his face (Revelation 22:4). Whatever is good in this world will be there, freed from the curse, and Christ will be its light.

If this world will be dissolved, does it matter what I do with it now? Yes, very much. The new creation is this creation renewed, not discarded, so faithful work done in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Caring for creation, doing justice, raising children, making things well, healing the sick: all of it honours the God who will renew the earth. What will not survive is sin, and whatever was done for self rather than for God (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). So hold this world loosely and serve it diligently: loosely, because it is passing; diligently, because it is his.

What it does not mean. Hastening does not mean we control God’s timetable or can force his hand. It means God uses his people’s prayers, holiness and witness in bringing about his purposes.

On a Tuesday. Pray your kingdom come today, and mean it: the Spirit, God’s pledge of that new world, already lives in you. Then choose one concrete act of holiness for today: an apology, an honest word, a generous gift, a conversation about Christ with someone who does not know him. Each one is a brick in a house that will not burn.

For worship. The fire is not the end. Beyond the roar and the melting is the promise: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home, and where the Lord who was a stranger in his own world, and had no home of his own in it, will dwell with his people for ever. He will wipe away every tear with his own hand. Everything Isaiah longed for, everything the martyrs died hoping for, he has promised, and he does not lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you are waiting for these. Everything Peter now asks flows from that expectation. People who expect a wedding prepare for it.

Without spot or blemish, and at peace. Be diligent, spoudasate, is the letter’s word for earnest, grace-driven effort (1:5, 10). Found, heurethēnai, picks up the word from verse 10, where the earth and its works are laid bare: everything will be found out, so be diligent about what is found in you. Without spot and blemish is another deliberate reversal: like Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19), and the opposite of the false teachers, who are blots and blemishes at the church’s own feast (2:13). At peace: with God through Christ (Romans 5:1), and with one another.

How can I be found without spot or blemish when I still sin? In two ways. First, by standing in Christ: his spotless righteousness is counted as yours, and his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). On that day you will be found in him, not having a righteousness of your own (Philippians 3:9). Second, by growing in holiness now, which is the fruit and evidence of being in him. Peter calls for diligence, not perfection. Keep short accounts with God, confess sin promptly, make peace with those you have wronged, and pursue holiness from a heart at rest in Christ’s finished work. He will present you blameless (Jude 24).

Count the patience of our Lord as salvation. Verse 9 restated as a command. Count, hēgeisthe, is the accounting verb. The scoffers count it slowness (v. 9); believers count it salvation, entering the interval on the right side of the ledger. Every day Christ has not yet come is another day in which someone you love can still turn to him, and in which you yourself are being made ready (v. 14).

Our beloved brother Paul. Peter’s warmth here is striking. These two men had a serious public disagreement at Antioch, where Paul opposed him to his face and later told the story in a letter the churches read (Galatians 2:11–14). Peter calls him beloved brother and commends his wisdom, inspired wisdom from God. There is no trace of the quarrel. That is what grace does to an old wound. Paul also taught about God’s patience leading to repentance (Romans 2:4; 9:22) and Christ’s return, and Peter knew several of his letters, which agreed with his own on these matters.

Hard to understand. Dysnoēta, difficult to grasp. It is an honest admission from an apostle about another apostle, and a small comfort to anyone who has struggled through Romans. Some of Paul’s teaching, perhaps on grace, freedom, election, or the last things, requires careful thought.

Twist to their own destruction. Ignorant, amatheis, is untaught; unstable, astēriktoi, not established, as in 2:14. Twist, streblousin, is to wrench, torture as on a rack: making a text say what it never meant by force. The false teachers twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into a licence for immorality (Romans 3:8; 6:1). Difficulty is not the cause of the twisting: the ignorant and unstable are, and they do it to the plain parts too.

The other Scriptures. Peter already counts Paul’s letters among the Scriptures, alongside the Old Testament. Many scholars see this as a sign of a later date, when Paul’s letters had been gathered into a collection. But Paul’s letters were copied and passed between churches in his own lifetime (Colossians 4:16), and Peter speaks only of the letters he knows. If, as this commentary holds, Peter wrote this, Paul was very likely still alive or, if the early tradition of his death under Nero is right, only lately martyred. Either way it is an early testimony to the recognition of the New Testament as inspired Scripture: the New Testament recognising itself.

How can I avoid twisting Scripture? Read whole passages, not isolated verses, and ask what the author meant to his first readers before asking what it means for you. Let clear passages interpret harder ones. Read with the church: good preaching, sound commentaries, and the confessions of faith keep you from private eccentricities. Be especially careful when an interpretation happens to excuse what you already wanted to do; that was exactly the false teachers’ method. And come to the Bible humbly, ready to be corrected by it rather than to use it.

What it does not mean. Hard to understand does not mean Scripture is unclear in its main message, or that ordinary believers cannot read it. The gospel is clear (Psalm 19:7). It means some passages require careful, humble study, and that we must not twist them to suit ourselves.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone with whom you are not at peace, perhaps a fellow believer who once rebuked you publicly, as Paul did Peter? Christ has made your peace with God, so follow Peter’s example: speak of them warmly, and seek peace.

verseByVerse.quote: You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing this beforehand. Proginōskontes, being forewarned: the whole letter’s purpose in a phrase. Peter has not written to inform them about the future but to prepare them, and forewarning is itself the protection.

Take care that you are not carried away. Take care, phylassesthe, is a sentry’s word. Carried away, synapachthentes, is swept along with, as a crowd sweeps along a man who did not intend to go. It is the word Paul used of Barnabas being carried away by Peter’s hypocrisy at Antioch (Galatians 2:13). Peter knew from his own failure how easily a good man is swept along, and how easily he can sweep others. Lawless, athesmōn, is the word used of the men of Sodom (2:7).

Lose your own stability. Stability, stērigmos, is from the same root as established (1:12) and unstable (v. 16; 2:14). A word has run through the letter: the unstable souls the false teachers baited (2:14), and the unstable who twist the Scriptures (3:16). Peter’s fear is that the steady will be pulled into that instability. And it is the word Jesus gave him: when you have turned again, strengthen (stērison) your brothers (Luke 22:32). His last sentence is still obeying that command.

But grow in the grace and knowledge. Then the last command, and after two chapters of warning it is not what one expects. Grow, auxanete, is present tense: keep growing. Peter does not end by telling them to watch the heretics more closely; he tells them to get on with maturing. A tree that is growing is far harder to uproot than one being braced. And both nouns matter. Grace is God’s unmerited favour, experienced more and more deeply, because a man who forgets he was cleansed stops growing (1:9). Knowledge is personal knowledge of Christ (1:2–3, 8), the letter’s key word, reclaimed one last time from the men who were peddling a counterfeit. The answer to false knowledge is not less knowledge but the real thing, and it is knowledge of a person. The letter ends where it began (1:2).

How do I actually grow in grace? Grace is not a substance you collect but the favour of God in Christ, known more deeply. You grow in it by using the means God has given: his word read, heard and preached; prayer; the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church; and obedience, which opens the heart to know him more (John 14:21). You also grow through suffering and repentance, as each fresh sight of your need shows you more of his kindness. Growth is slow and often unseen, like a tree. Do not measure it day by day. Keep near the sources, and over years it will show.

What it does not mean. Lose your stability does not mean true believers can finally fall away. Peter has said they will never fall if they grow (1:10). The warning is one of God’s means to keep them standing.

To him be the glory. To Jesus Christ: a doxology offering him the glory due to God alone, who says, my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8). It is a final testimony to his deity; the letter began by calling him our God and Saviour (1:1), and it ends by giving him God’s glory. Day of eternity, hēmera aiōnos, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: the eternal day that begins at his return and never ends. Peter, having written a chapter about the day of the Lord and the day of judgement, ends by naming a day that has no evening. If, as this commentary holds, Peter wrote them, these are the last recorded words of the man who denied his Lord in a courtyard, written when he knew his death was near.

For worship. The last word of Peter is glory, and the glory is Christ’s. The fisherman who sank in the waves, who cursed and swore that he did not know him, who was found and forgiven on a beach at dawn, ends his life giving that same Lord the glory that belongs to God alone. That is what grace does. It takes a man who denied Jesus and sends him to his cross singing doxology. To our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ be the glory, now, in the long patience of this age, and on the day of eternity that will never end. Amen.

3.theology:
The word of God and the uniform world: The scoffers claim that the world runs on unbroken natural regularity (v. 4). Peter grants the observation and points to two interruptions in the very history they appeal to: creation and the flood, both brought about by the word of God. The same word has spoken of a third act, the fire, and it is as certain as the first two.

Divine patience and salvation: Verse 9 says God is “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” Reformed theology reads it in its setting: he is patient “toward you”, the chosen community, and the delay is the time in which all who will repent are gathered. This is not universalism, for the day will still come and shut the door, and it does not contradict election, for God’s patience is the means by which the elect are gathered. The apparent delay of Christ’s coming is not procrastination but love at work.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 are the horizon of the whole letter. Herman Bavinck’s axiom, grace restores nature, applies here: the fire purifies creation rather than abolishing it, and the new creation is this creation glorified. Anthony Hoekema’s The Bible and the Future argues that the new earth is a renewal, not a replacement, which is why Christian hope is not escapism: the world we tend and serve matters, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
3.examples:
Then: The scoffers’ question, “Where is the promise of his coming?”, has been asked in every generation since the first believers died. Peter’s answer stands for each of them: God is not slow but patient, and his patience is mercy, gathering those still to be gathered before the door closes.

Now: “What sort of people ought you to be” (v. 11) is the letter’s most searching question. A person who believes the day is coming will live differently: with moral seriousness, with urgency about the gospel, loose to the world’s false securities, and longing for righteousness. The last word is not a warning but a gift: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
